# ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery

Yongqiang Chen^(\*$`\dagger`$) Affiliation: MBZUAI Affiliation: Carnegie
Mellon University    Chenxi Liu^(\*) Affiliation: TMLR Group, Hong Kong
Baptist University    Deyu Zou^(\*) Affiliation: The Chinese University
of Hong Kong    Zhenhao Chen Affiliation: MBZUAI    Tongliang Liu
Affiliation: MBZUAI Affiliation: SAIC Centre, The University of Sydney
   Bo Han Affiliation: TMLR Group, Hong Kong Baptist University    Kun
Zhang Affiliation: MBZUAI Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University

###### Abstract

Evolutionary coding agents such as AlphaEvolve are one of the notable
successes in using Large Language Models (LLMs) to build AI Scientists.
These agents tackle open-ended scientific problems by iteratively
improving and evolving programs, leveraging the prior knowledge and
reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Despite their success, mutations over
programs are mostly low-level upon surface heuristics, without a
persistent unit of control. In contrast, science compounds through
ideas. In this work, we propose ExpEvolve, which injects idea-level
extraction and control into evolution: it discovers and leverages the
high-level factors from programs that explain scoring differences among
different programs. We characterize theoretical conditions on when
discovery with idea factors improves sample efficiency. We also build a
practical framework to show that the extracted high-level idea factors
are helpful for guiding exploitation from experience and exploration
when discovery comes to a plateau. Across $`11`$ open-ended mathematical
tasks, ExpEvolve significantly improves the final performance and sample
efficiency up to $`5.0\times`$. The improvements also transfer to $`4`$
other LLMs and to $`6`$ machine learning tasks from MLS-Bench. Analysis
shows that ExpEvolve can discover idea-level factors to provide better
exploration and exploitation for evolutionary discovery.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are now widely used to build agents that
operate on increasingly long-horizon tasks ([Plaat et al.,
2025](#bib.bib68)). One of the most ambitious applications is AI
scientist agents ([Zheng et al., 2025a](#bib.bib112)), in which LLMs
automate the scientific discovery process, including literature surveys
([Asai et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)), hypothesis generation ([Wang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib94); [Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib104)), data-driven
analysis ([Majumder et al., 2025](#bib.bib56)), experiment design ([Li
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib40)), or even the whole discovery workflow ([Lu
et al., 2024](#bib.bib50); [Yamada et al., 2025](#bib.bib100); [Gottweis
et al., 2026](#bib.bib24); [Mitchener et al., 2025](#bib.bib58)).
LLM-driven discovery has shown strong results in a variety of domains,
such as mathematics ([OpenAI, 2026c](#bib.bib64); [OpenAI,
2026b](#bib.bib63)), de novo protein design ([Anthropic,
2026](#bib.bib2)), algorithm discovery ([Novikov et al.,
2025](#bib.bib61); [Lange et al., 2026](#bib.bib37)), and the research
that develops LLMs themselves, an early form of recursive
self-improvement (RSI) ([OpenAI, 2026a](#bib.bib62); [Favaro and Clark,
2026](#bib.bib16); [Lyu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib54); [Karpathy,
2026](#bib.bib33)). At the heart of the discovery loop is the iteration
over scientific hypotheses, where scientific ideas compound throughout
the evaluation of promising hypotheses ([Wallace et al.,
2026](#bib.bib90)). Therefore, it is essential to reuse the discovery
experience to generate high-quality hypotheses, e.g., avoiding getting
stuck in repetitive mistakes or suboptimal solutions and encoding
promising exploratory proposals.

In this work, we study experience reuse in open-ended discovery with
evolutionary coding agents, where hypotheses are represented as solution
programs to the underlying scientific problem, and experiences are
accumulated as evaluated programs and their scores given by an explicit
evaluator ([Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib61)). Typically, existing
evolutionary coding agents such as ShinkaEvolve directly incorporate
successful programs or rely on LLMs to summarize reusable insights and
incorporate them as memory for future mutations with LLMs ([Lange et
al., 2026](#bib.bib37); [Gideoni et al., 2026](#bib.bib22); [Karpathy,
2026](#bib.bib33)). However, program mutation contains an open-ended
search space including low-level details such as hyperparameters and
high-level insights such as optimization strategies. LLM-driven guidance
is prone to focusing on low-level details ([Karpathy, 2026](#bib.bib33);
[Pelleriti et al., 2026](#bib.bib66)), which may not bring genuine new
scientific discoveries. In contrast, human scientists tend to recognize
the high-level contrasts among programs, accumulate and exploit
scientific ideas from experience ([Kuhn and Hawkins, 1963](#bib.bib36);
[Douven, 2025](#bib.bib15)). The gap raises a challenging research
question:

> How can we reuse experience for evolutionary discovery like human
> scientists?

To tackle the question, we formulate evolutionary discovery as a
Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) ([Kaelbling et al.,
1998](#bib.bib32)) (Sec.
[3](#S3 "3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")).
In each turn, the agent needs to propose meaningful solutions to uncover
the underlying causal mechanism for solving the scientific problem,
i.e., maximizing the evaluation score ([Wallace, 1981](#bib.bib91);
[Glymour,](#bib.bib23) ). Under the formulation, we introduce the notion
of ideas as high-level mechanistic properties of the programs that
determine the evaluation scores, e.g., the construction family or the
optimization strategy (Def.
[3.2](#S3.Thmtheorem2 "Definition 3.2 (Idea). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")).
Without uncovering the ideas, the agent has to treat programs as
unrelated and cannot tell whether a revision changes an idea or only a
low-level detail, so discovery degenerates into exhaustive search (Thm.
[3.1](#S3.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 3.1 (Structured experience reuse, informal). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")).
Meanwhile, the identification of ideas also requires sufficient
exploration to contrast programs with and without each idea (Thm.
[3.3](#S3.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 3.3 (Degenerated exploration of ideas). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")).
Hence, an effective discovery agent needs to extract ideas from
experience, and keep exploring programs where the ideas vary.

![Refer to caption](2610.29303v1/idea_evolution_illustration.png)

Figure 1: Comparison between experience reuse at program-level and
idea-level. All programs solve the same grid task. Left: Experience
reuse at program-level is prone to low-level edits. Program-level
evolution derives new programs from a high-scoring parent, such as
changing the heuristic weight or bounding the search loop. Both edited
programs score lower. Right: Experience reuse at idea-level compares
structurally different programs through a shared procedure-level factor,
lp = refine_lp(lp). Programs that contain the factor score higher than
the program that omits it. This contrast singles out the factor, which
is then inserted into new programs of different structures.

Motivated by the analysis, we propose ExpEvolve, which recognizes,
structures, and leverages the high-level idea factors from discovery
experience (Fig.
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")).
Specifically, ExpEvolve realizes the discovery of ideas via identifying
high-level factors that help explain the program scoring differences.
Built upon COAT ([Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib47)), the discovered idea
factors are expected to predict which program performs better given any
pair of programs in the experience. Then, the admitted idea factors will
be incorporated as an action of a multi-armed bandit that controls the
exploration and exploitation of different ideas during discovery. To
enable sufficient exploration, ExpEvolve also allocates slots for random
exploration ([Gideoni et al., 2026](#bib.bib22)), and idea-guided
exploration when the evolution comes to a plateau. The idea-guided
exploration enforces LLMs to explore diverse ideas other than those
widely used in top-scoring programs. The idea-based control in ExpEvolve
allows efficient exploitation of promising ideas while continuing to
explore programs with varied ideas.

We evaluate ExpEvolve on $`11`$ open-ended mathematical discovery tasks
with a budget of $`200`$ evaluated programs, using SCS as the backbone
and the main baseline (Sec.
[5](#S5 "5 Experiments ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")).
Under two configurations that split the budget into $`20`$ generations
of $`10`$ programs and $`10`$ generations of $`20`$ programs, ExpEvolve
improves the final performance over SCS and ShinkaEvolve in most
settings with smaller budgets up to $`5.0\times`$. Further analyses show
that the discovered idea factors order the archived programs better than
their code length on all $`11`$ tasks. We further integrate ExpEvolve
into OpenRSI ([Yang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib102)) on six tasks from
MLS-Bench ([Lyu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib54)), where it improves the mean
final best-so-far score of OpenRSI on all six tasks.

## 2 Related Work

In this section, we discuss the closest related works and defer a more
detailed one in Appendix
[B](#A2 "Appendix B Related Work ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").

AI Scientist agents. With the significant advancement in LLM capacity
and the development of agentic systems, building LLM-based AI scientists
has gained increasing attention ([Zhou et al., 2025](#bib.bib115)). One
research line automates part or the whole of the pipelines in scientific
activities through agentic workflows ([Lu et al., 2026](#bib.bib51);
[Yamada et al., 2025](#bib.bib100); [Gottweis et al., 2026](#bib.bib24);
[Ghareeb et al., 2026](#bib.bib21); [Mitchener et al.,
2025](#bib.bib58); [Feng et al., 2026b](#bib.bib18); [Lyu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib55)). Evolutionary coding agents are one of the most
representative AI scientist agents that integrate LLMs into evolutionary
search over programs scored by an explicit evaluator ([Romera-Paredes et
al., 2024](#bib.bib71); [Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib61)). AI
scientist agents, including evolutionary coding agents, have made impact
in a variety of domains, such as mathematics ([OpenAI,
2026b](#bib.bib63)), materials science ([Ghafarollahi and Buehler,
2025](#bib.bib20)), biology ([Anthropic, 2026](#bib.bib2)), and the
development of LLMs themselves, e.g., accelerating LLM training and
research toward recursive self-improvement ([Karpathy,
2026](#bib.bib33); [Lyu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib54); [OpenAI,
2026a](#bib.bib62); [Favaro and Clark, 2026](#bib.bib16); [Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib110)). As generation scales up, validating the generated
hypotheses becomes the main cost ([Wallace et al., 2026](#bib.bib90)),
and ideas that look promising often degrade once executed ([Si et al.,
2026](#bib.bib79)). The expanding paradigm of LLM-driven scientific
discovery makes the reuse of experience increasingly more essential,
which is central to our work.

Experience reuse in evolutionary coding agents. Existing evolutionary
coding agents typically reuse experience via conditioning on evaluated
programs ([Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib61); [Gideoni et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22)) or summarizing textual insights from programs into
memory for future mutations ([Lange et al., 2026](#bib.bib37); [Liu et
al., 2024](#bib.bib48); [Ye et al., 2024](#bib.bib106); [Volkov et al.,
2026](#bib.bib89)). The useful experience can also be exploited for
future search control, e.g., selection inspirations across diverse
strategy clusters ([Lange et al., 2026](#bib.bib37); [Luo et al.,
2026](#bib.bib52)). Different from existing works that concentrate on
the unit of experience as texts or programs, ExpEvolve discovers and
exploits high-level idea factors to guide program mutations.

## 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery

In this section, we formalize evolutionary discovery and introduce the
notion of ideas.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 2: Evolutionary discovery as a POMDP. (A) In each iteration, an
evolutionary coding agent builds the proposal context from its memory,
e.g., parent and inspiration programs or summarized insights, and
generates candidate programs with an LLM $`G`$. The evaluator scores
every program, whose outcome depends on the hidden mechanism
$`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$, and the scored programs enter the archive and
update the memory. (B) The corresponding temporal graphical model. The
memory $`m_{t}`$ guides the next program $`p_{t}`$, and the score
$`y_{t}`$ depends on both $`p_{t}`$ and the static but unknown mechanism
$`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$, which in turn updates $`m_{t+1}`$.

### 3.1 Evolutionary Discovery as a POMDP

Scientific discovery aims to uncover the causal mechanisms underlying a
problem through interactions with the world ([Kuhn and Hawkins,
1963](#bib.bib36)). In evolutionary discovery, the agent interacts with
the problem through an evaluator. We denote by
$`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}\in\Theta`$ the hidden mechanism of the problem,
which is fixed during the search and unknown to the agent. At turn
$`t`$, the agent proposes a program $`p_{t}\in\mathcal{P}`$ and observes
a score $`y_{t}`$ with
$`\mathbb{E}[y_{t}\mid p_{t}]=F(p_{t};\theta_{\mathrm{sci}})`$, where
$`F:\mathcal{P}\times\Theta\to\mathbb{R}`$ is the objective, e.g., the
value of a mathematical construction, the efficiency of a kernel, or the
performance of a trained model ([Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib61)). The
goal is to uncover $`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$ by optimizing for the
evaluation score.

POMDP. As shown in Fig.
[2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")B,
the interaction forms a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process
(POMDP) ([Kaelbling et al., 1998](#bib.bib32)) with a static hidden
state $`s_{t}=\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$, actions $`a_{t}=p_{t}`$,
observations $`o_{t}=y_{t}`$, an identity transition kernel, and the
observation kernel $`O(y_{t}\mid\theta_{\mathrm{sci}},p_{t})`$. Given a
budget of $`T`$ evaluations, the agent chooses $`p_{0},\dots,p_{T-1}`$
to find a program $`\hat{p}`$ with high
$`F(\hat{p};\theta_{\mathrm{sci}})`$.

Evaluation as intervention. $`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$ can be
parameterized as a structural causal model over variables of interest
([Spirtes et al., 2000](#bib.bib82)), in which a program specifies a
configuration $`x_{p}`$ of design variables $`X`$. Each evaluation can
be considered as the expected outcome of the intervention:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
F(p;\theta_{\mathrm{sci}})=\mathbb{E}\big[\,Y\,\big|\,\mathrm{do}(X=x_{p}),\ \theta_{\mathrm{sci}}\big].
``` |  | (1) |

In this work, we leverage the causal view to provide a more in-depth
understanding, while neither the analysis nor the method requires
recovering the causal graph. A full discussion on the relations with
causality can be found in Appendix
[C](#A3 "Appendix C A Causal View of the Formulation ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").

Experience-driven discovery. We define $`b_{t}`$ as the agent’s Bayesian
belief after accumulating experience
$`h_{t}=\{(p_{0},y_{0}),\dots,(p_{t-1},y_{t-1})\}`$, which is
essentially a probability distribution on $`\Theta`$,
$`b_{t}(B)=\Pr(\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}}\in B\mid h_{t})`$ for
$`B\subseteq\Theta`$. In the ideal Bayesian formalism, the belief
$`b_{t}`$ is a sufficient statistic for decision-making ([Kaelbling et
al., 1998](#bib.bib32)). In practice, the AI Scientist maintains an
internal belief within LLMs, or an external one realized as memory
$`m_{t}=\Phi(h_{t})`$ for some (possibly learnable) summarization
function $`\Phi`$ ([Lange et al., 2026](#bib.bib37)), to represent the
*approximate representation* of its knowledge about
$`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$ and the landscape of
$`F(\cdot;\theta_{\mathrm{sci}})`$. Each evaluation step
$`(p_{t},y_{t})`$ thus updates $`m_{t}`$, which in turn updates the
agent’s belief about $`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$ and determines the next
action $`p_{t+1}`$.

### 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas

If the evaluator fully reveals $`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$ and the
evaluation budget is unlimited, then enumerating every possible program
can directly lead to discovery. However, in reality, the evaluation
score only reveals partial information about $`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$
and evaluations can be expensive, e.g., training a model or running a
physical experiment, so the agent can afford only a limited number of
them ([Wallace et al., 2026](#bib.bib90)). Therefore, it is essential to
reuse experience from past evaluations.

Without properly reusing experience, a single evaluation cannot reveal
further insights about other unseen programs, and the agent then has to
evaluate every candidate program to find the best one. Reusing
experience requires some structure shared across programs, so that the
evaluation of one program also informs the others. We formalize the
contrast as follows.

###### Theorem 3.1 (Structured experience reuse, informal).

Let $`\mathcal{P}=\{p_{1},\dots,p_{K}\}`$, and let each evaluation
return $`y_{t}=F(p_{t};\theta_{\mathrm{sci}})+\varepsilon_{t}`$ with
$`\varepsilon_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})`$ i.i.d.

1.  (a)
    *With reuse.* If each program has a known representation
    $`\phi(p)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}`$ with $`\|\phi(p)\|_{2}\leq 1`$ and
    $`F(p;\theta_{\mathrm{sci}})=\langle\phi(p),w^{\star}\rangle`$ for
    an unknown $`w^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}`$, then under a coverage
    condition on the representation, there exists a policy that, with
    probability at least $`1-\delta`$, outputs a program within
    $`\epsilon`$ of the optimal value after
    $`O\big(d\,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\log\frac{K}{\delta}\big)`$
    evaluations.
2.  (b)
    *Without reuse.* If programs are unrelated, i.e.,
    $`F(p_{i};\theta_{\mathrm{sci}})=\mu_{i}`$ for an arbitrary
    $`\mu\in\mathbb{R}^{K}`$, then any policy with the same guarantee
    for every $`\mu`$ needs
    $`\Omega\big(K\,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\log\frac{1}{\delta}\big)`$
    evaluations.

The formal statement and proof are given in Appendix
[E](#A5 "Appendix E Proof of Theorem (Structured experience reuse) ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").
Theorem
[3.1](#S3.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 3.1 (Structured experience reuse, informal). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
implies that reusing experience at the high-level design choices can
significantly improve sample efficiency from $`\Omega(K)`$ to
$`O(d\log K)`$, where $`K\gg d`$. In evolutionary discovery, $`K`$
counts the candidate program space, which grow combinatorially with the
high-level design choices and further with the ways of implementing each
choice, while $`d`$ is determined by the design choices that affect the
score. Most existing agents retain experience at the level of programs
([Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib61); [Lange et al., 2026](#bib.bib37)),
which ignores the high-level design choices. In contrast, human
scientists recognize and record what they learn from experiments in
terms of reusable concepts, e.g., a construction or an optimization
technique, which carry over to later experiments. We are hence inspired
to introduce the notion of ideas.

###### Definition 3.2 (Idea).

An idea is an interpretable mapping $`z:\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{V}`$ from
programs to a binary or categorical value. It describes a high-level
mechanistic property that can be shared by syntactically different
programs, such as the construction family, initialization, or
optimization procedure. A set of ideas $`\{z_{1},\dots,z_{r}\}`$ defines
the idea representation $`Z(p)=(z_{1}(p),\dots,z_{r}(p))`$.

A program realizes a set of ideas together with low-level details. We
call an idea representation $`Z`$ *faithful* if the score depends on a
program only through its ideas, i.e.,
$`F(p;\theta_{\mathrm{sci}})=g(Z(p))`$ for some function $`g`$
determined by $`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$. Under a faithful idea
representation, the hidden mechanism acts on a program only through its
ideas, and Theorem
[3.1](#S3.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 3.1 (Structured experience reuse, informal). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
applies with $`\phi(p)`$ being the one-hot encoding of $`Z(p)`$, whose
dimension is determined by the number of ideas.

Identifiability of ideas. However, the agent does not know in advance
which representation is faithful, and the ideas have to be identified
from the evaluated programs, while which programs are evaluated is
decided by the search itself. When the search stops varying the
candidate ideas, the exploration of ideas degenerates, as formalized
below.

###### Theorem 3.3 (Degenerated exploration of ideas).

Consider two candidate ideas $`z_{0}`$ and $`z_{1}`$, and two mechanisms
$`\theta_{0}`$ and $`\theta_{1}`$ under which the score depends on
$`z_{0}`$ and $`z_{1}`$, respectively, i.e.,
$`F(p;\theta_{i})=g(Z(p),z_{i}(p))`$ for a common representation $`Z`$
and function $`g`$, with the same observation noise. Suppose the optimal
programs under $`\theta_{0}`$ and $`\theta_{1}`$ are different and
unique with a margin $`\Delta>0`$. Then for any policy that only
evaluates programs on which $`z_{0}`$ and $`z_{1}`$ agree, there exists
$`i\in\{0,1\}`$ such that for every budget $`T`$, the output $`\hat{p}`$
satisfies
$`\mathbb{E}\big[\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}F(p;\theta_{i})-F(\hat{p};\theta_{i})\big]\geq\Delta/2`$.

The formal statement and proof are given in Appendix
[F](#A6 "Appendix F Proof of Theorem (Degenerated exploration of ideas) ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").
Theorem
[3.3](#S3.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 3.3 (Degenerated exploration of ideas). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
can be considered as a consequence of the partial observability of
$`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$, since the scores reveal
$`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$ only through the evaluated programs. If two
candidate ideas agree on all explored programs, the two mechanisms
produce the same observations, and one cannot distinguish which idea
determines the score. This situation is common in evolutionary search:
as the search concentrates around its current best programs, the ideas
shared by these programs stop varying. Identifying ideas thus requires
sufficient exploration to contrast programs with and without each idea,
to isolate contributions of ideas in the program space.

## 4 ExpEvolve: Discovering and Exploiting Ideas from Experience

Theoretical analysis in Sec.
[3](#S3 "3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
suggests that a discovery agent should extract ideas from its
experience, and keep exploring programs where the ideas vary. We realize
the theoretical principles in ExpEvolve. The full procedure and
implementation details are given in Alg.
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
and Appendix
[H](#A8 "Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").

### 4.1 Discovering Ideas from Experience

We leverage the discovery loop of the COAT framework ([Liu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib47)) to find idea factors according to their theoretical
properties.

![Refer to caption](2610.29303v1/idea_discovery.png)

Figure 3: Illustration of idea factor discovery.

Idea memory. During the discovery, ExpEvolve maintains an idea memory
$`\mathcal{M}_{t}`$ which is a set of idea factors. Each idea factor is
stored with a name, a description of its code pattern, a type, i.e.,
binary or categorical, and a value set $`\mathcal{V}`$. For each program
in the experience archive, the values of idea factors are annotated by
an annotator LLM, which instantiates the idea representation $`Z(p)`$.

Explainability of idea factors. A faithful idea representation is
expected to be able to predict the score of a program, i.e.,
$`F(p;\theta_{\mathrm{sci}})=g(Z(p))`$ (Sec.
[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")).
However, predicting the exact scores from ideas is difficult, since the
scores of different tasks lie on different scales, the unknown function
$`g`$ can be highly nonlinear, and the archive only contains a limited
number of noisy evaluations. Therefore, we define the explainability of
an idea representation by its pairwise predictability, i.e., whether
$`Z(p)`$ and $`Z(p^{\prime})`$ predict which of two programs $`p`$ and
$`p^{\prime}`$ is better. The ranking is already informative for
optimizing the objective, invariant to the scale of the scores, and more
robust to noise than the scores.

Discovering idea factors from unexplained pairs. The idea discovery
process in ExpEvolve is an iterative loop: each time the discovery is
triggered, ExpEvolve fits a pairwise ranker on the annotated idea
factors, and selects the pairs of archived programs with a large score
gap that the current idea factors fail to explain. The unexplained pairs
suggest the existence of missing idea factors that separate the programs
in each pair. For the selected pairs, a separate proposer LLM reads the
programs to propose candidate idea factors that distinguish them. Each
candidate is then annotated on the whole archive, and is admitted into
the idea memory if each of its values is supported by enough programs
and its values separate the scores.

Figure 4: Illustration of two-level exploration-exploitation with
discovered idea factors.

### 4.2 Exploiting Idea Factors for Discovery

We build a two-level exploration and exploitation framework with a
multi-armed bandit (MAB) to fully exploit discovered idea factors while
exploring varying design spaces.

Exploration and MAB exploitation. In each generation, ExpEvolve keeps at
least a fraction $`\rho`$ of the slots for random exploration that
follows SCS ([Gideoni et al., 2026](#bib.bib22)) with randomly sampled
example programs, which explores programs beyond the current ideas and
provides new material for discovery. The remaining slots are allocated
to idea-guided actions by MAB.

![Refer to caption](2610.29303v1/idea_pleateau.png)

Figure 5: Illustration of idea-guided exploration at plateaus.

Idea factors as MAB actions. To exploit an idea factor $`z`$, ExpEvolve
compiles it into edit actions, e.g., $`\mathsf{ADD}(z)`$ and
$`\mathsf{REMOVE}(z)`$ for a binary idea factor. An action adds to the
context an instruction that describes $`z`$, together with demonstration
programs in the target state, to ask the mutator LLM to realize the
action in the new program. The MAB selects the action for each
idea-guided slot. The reward of an action is the score of the program
generated under the action relative to the random exploration in the
same generation,
i.e.,$`r=\frac{y-\bar{y}_{\mathrm{rand}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{rand}}},`$
where $`y`$ is the score of the generated program, and
$`\bar{y}_{\mathrm{rand}}`$ and $`\sigma_{\mathrm{rand}}`$ are the mean
and the standard deviation of the scores of random exploration in the
same generation. The normalization removes the drift of scores across
generations and the differences of score scales across tasks. The MAB
selects the actions with an upper confidence bound (UCB) rule on the
maximum reward of each action (Appendix
[H.3](#A8.SS3 "H.3 Idea-Guided Actions ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")).

Exploration at plateaus. Oftentimes, evolutionary discovery can
concentrate around its best programs and a single strategy.
Consequently, the ideas widely used in top-scoring programs stop
varying, and their roles cannot be identified from the archive (Thm.
[3.3](#S3.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 3.3 (Degenerated exploration of ideas). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")).
When the best score does not improve for $`\kappa`$ generations,
ExpEvolve switches to idea-guided exploration, which enforces the
mutator LLM to explore diverse ideas other than those widely used in
top-scoring programs. Specifically, a separate LLM probes the properties
shared by the top-scoring programs as background idea factors, and an
LLM judge determines which idea factors in the memory depend on the
background. ExpEvolve then masks the actions of the dependent idea
factors, instructs the mutator LLM to avoid them, and assigns more slots
to random exploration with diversified demonstrations.

## 5 Experiments

We evaluate ExpEvolve on $`11`$ open-ended mathematical discovery tasks
and further integrate it into an evolutionary agent for Machine Learning
Engineering (MLE) tasks.

### 5.1 Experimental Setup

Tasks. We evaluate on $`11`$ open-ended mathematical discovery tasks.
Nine tasks are the problems studied by SCS ([Gideoni et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22)), which are taken from AlphaEvolve ([Novikov et al.,
2025](#bib.bib61)), including the first and second autocorrelation
inequalities, the uncertainty inequality, the Erdős minimum overlap
problem, sums and differences of sets, the max–min distance ratio, the
Heilbronn problem for triangles, the kissing number in $`11`$
dimensions, and circle packing. The other two tasks are the Hadamard
matrix problem ([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib96)) and a variant of circle
packing that recovers the radii by linear programming. We report the
best score at the end of the budget, as the mean and standard deviation
over seeds, and the best seed. Full details of the tasks are given in
Appendix
[I.1](#A9.SS1 "I.1 Tasks ‣ Appendix I Experimental Details ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").

Budget. Each run evaluates $`200`$ programs. We consider two
configurations with the same budget, i.e., $`10`$ generations of $`20`$
programs as in SCS ([Gideoni et al., 2026](#bib.bib22)) and $`20`$
generations of $`10`$ programs, which presents more challenges to
accumulating reusable knowledge from experience.

Implementation. We compare ExpEvolve with SCS ([Gideoni et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22)), which is the backbone of ExpEvolve and shows
competitive results against more elaborate evolutionary coding agents.
We further compare with ShinkaEvolve ([Lange et al., 2026](#bib.bib37)),
which maintains an island-based archive and summarizes the insights of
recent programs with a meta-summary. Details are given in Appendix
[I.2](#A9.SS2 "I.2 Baselines ‣ Appendix I Experimental Details ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").
We use DeepSeek-V4-Flash by default, and each setting is run with $`3`$
seeds. ExpEvolve uses a random-exploration fraction $`\rho=0.60`$ for
$`20`$-gen. and $`\rho=0.40`$ for $`10`$-gen. to keep a similar number
of random-exploration slots, i.e., $`6`$ and $`8`$. We donot tune other
hyperparameters.

ExpEvolve consistently improves the final performance. Table
[1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
shows the final performance at the budget of $`200`$ programs. ExpEvolve
improves the mean and best final performances across most settings over
SCS and ShinkaEvolve. Moreover, the improvements are robust to how the
budget is parallelized. From $`10`$ generations of $`20`$ programs to
$`20`$ generations of $`10`$ programs, the mean final score of SCS can
drop dramatically because of limited capability in experience reuse,
while ExpEvolve still maintains competitive performance. More details
are given in Appendix
[J](#A10 "Appendix J Additional Results ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").

Figure 6: Best-so-far scores along the budget of $`200`$ evaluated
programs.

ExpEvolve improves sample efficiency. Fig.
[6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
shows the best-so-far scores along the budget on Hadamard, Sums and
differences, Heilbronn, and Minimum overlap. On these four tasks,
ExpEvolve needs $`1.7\times`$ to $`26.2\times`$ fewer evaluations than
SCS under both configurations.

Figure 7: (a) Best-so-far scores of SCS and ExpEvolve with other LLMs.
(b) Best-so-far scores of SCS, SCS+meta, and ExpEvolve.

The improvements transfer to other LLMs. Fig.
[7](#S5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
(a) shows that the advantages of ExpEvolve over SCS transfers to other
LLMs such as DeepSeek-v4-pro, GLM-5.2 and Gemini-3.7-Flash.

Summarizing experience as memory helps the early search but saturates.
ShinkaEvolve and SCS+meta retain the experience as a textual summary of
recent programs, which provides additional context to the mutator LLM
without controlling which ideas are evaluated. Fig.
[7](#S5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
(b) shows that SCS+meta improves over SCS in the early stage. However,
its improvement slows down afterwards while ExpEvolve keep improving. It
again verifies the advantages of idea-guided evolution.

The discovered idea factors explain the order of archived programs.
Following the definition of explainability in Sec.

we measure the fraction of archived program pairs that discovered
factors can order correctly. As shown in Fig.

the discovered idea factors reach an accuracy of $`0.79`$ to $`0.99`$.
Fig.
[8](#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")(b)
shows the idea factor with the largest weight on each task.

In an example run, idea-guided actions produce about half of the new
best programs. Fig.
[8](#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")(c)
shows a run on Sums and differences with $`10`$ generations of $`20`$

slots. The $`92`$ idea-guided slots of the run select $`7`$ distinct

### 5.3 Additional Experiments on Machine Learning Engineering Tasks

We further study whether the effectiveness of ExpEvolve transfers to MLE
by integrating it into OpenRSI ([Yang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib102)) and
evaluating it on $`6`$ tasks from MLS-Bench ([Lyu et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib54)): *Online bandit*, *Anomaly detection*, *Clustering*,
*Multi-objective optimization*, *Subgroup calibration shift*, and
*Evolution strategy*. Search leverages the scores and execution feedback
from each task.

Experimental setup. We use the evolutionary harness from OpenRSI, which
organizes search through Draft, Improve, Debug, and Crossover operators.
For each task, we retain a fixed history containing 20 completed search
slots from an earlier OpenRSI run. The OpenRSI baseline and OpenRSI
equipped with ExpEvolve continue from this same history for 50
additional evaluator calls, with 3 seeds. Both methods use 5 search
slots per generation. All program generation uses Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. The
same checkpoint performs factor discovery and annotation in ExpEvolve.
For each task and method, we average the final best-so-far (BSF) scores
over three seeds.

Idea-guided evolution transfers to MLE tasks. Fig.
[9(a)](#S5.F9.sf1 "In Figure 9 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
compares OpenRSI with OpenRSI+ExpEvolve across the six tasks, where
ExpEvolve shows superior performance on all six tasks, with the largest
gains on Online bandit and Anomaly detection.

Idea-guided actions produce better exploration and exploitation on MLE
tasks. Fig.
[9(b)](#S5.F9.sf2 "In Figure 9 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
and Fig.
[9(c)](#S5.F9.sf3 "In Figure 9 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
show two concrete trajectories in the tasks of multi-objective
optimization and evolution strategy, respectively. We can find that
ExpEvolve can effectively discover useful ideas such as removing running
ideal-point tracking (A1), removing reference-vector adaptation (A2),
and adding hybrid differential-evolution variation (A3) to effectively
boost the performance. When the evolution gets stuck at plateaus,
exploiting useful strategies proposed by ExpEvolve in multi-objective
optimization, or exploration guided by idea factors in ExpEvolve can
effectively break the plateaus and lead to improvements. More details
about the implementation can be found in Appendix
[K.1](#A11.SS1 "K.1 More Details of Experiments on Machine Learning Engineering ‣ Appendix K Prompts ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").

## 6 Conclusions

We introduced ExpEvolve, which structures the experience of evolutionary
discovery into idea factors and reuses them to guide the search.
ExpEvolve discovers idea factors from the pairs of programs that the
current idea factors fail to explain, exploits them as the actions of a
multi-armed bandit, and keeps exploring programs where the ideas vary,
through random exploration and idea-guided exploration at plateaus. Our
analysis shows that reusing a faithful idea representation reduces the
number of evaluations from $`\Omega(K)`$ to $`O(d\log K)`$, and that
identifying ideas requires exploring programs where the ideas vary. On
$`11`$ mathematical discovery tasks and $`6`$ tasks from MLS-Bench,
ExpEvolve improves the final performance and the sample efficiency of
evolutionary discovery under the same evaluation budget.
````
