````math
## Appendix A Limitations and Future directions

Due to the resource constraints, the tasks studied in this work remain
limited to small-scale verification and are relatively simple. There
remains a broader scope of scientific problems to be explored where
verification signals can be expensive, such as biology, medicine, etc..
Meanwhile, the factor discovery can also be guided with additional
background knowledge of the task.

## Appendix B Related Work

In this section, we present more detailed discussions of related works
in the literature.

AI Scientist agents. With the significant advancement in LLM capacity
and the development of agentic systems, a rising number of works develop
agents to help scientific discovery ([Zheng et al., 2025a](#bib.bib112);
[Zhou et al., 2025](#bib.bib115); [Tie et al., 2025](#bib.bib86)). Some
systems automate the whole research workflow, from idea generation to
experimentation and paper writing ([Lu et al., 2026](#bib.bib51);
[Yamada et al., 2025](#bib.bib100); [Gottweis et al., 2026](#bib.bib24);
[Ghareeb et al., 2026](#bib.bib21); [Mitchener et al.,
2025](#bib.bib58); [Feng et al., 2026b](#bib.bib18); [Lyu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib55)). One research line automates specific scientific
activities, including literature review and deep research ([Asai et al.,
2026](#bib.bib3); [Huang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib29)), hypothesis
generation ([Li et al., 2025c](#bib.bib42); [Yang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib104); [Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib94); [Yang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib105)), hypothesis verification ([Li et al.,
2024](#bib.bib43); [Huang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib28)), and feedback on
scientific papers ([Liang et al., 2024](#bib.bib46)). Another line
targets data-driven discovery and machine learning engineering
([Majumder et al., 2025](#bib.bib56); [Wang et al., 2025c](#bib.bib97);
[Jing et al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Chan et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)), as
well as embodied agents in self-driving laboratories that conduct
real-world experiments ([Roch et al., 2020](#bib.bib70); [Zhu et al.,
2022](#bib.bib116); [Tom et al., 2024](#bib.bib87); [Zhang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib111); [Mandal et al., 2025](#bib.bib57)). A growing set of
benchmarks evaluates the research abilities of these agents, e.g.,
replicating and conducting AI research ([Starace et al.,
2025](#bib.bib83); [Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib99); [Lyu et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib54)), generating hypotheses from inspirations ([Liu et
al., 2026](#bib.bib49)), discovering scientific laws and equations
([Zheng et al., 2026](#bib.bib113); [Shojaee et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib78)), and conducting research tasks in biology ([Laurent
et al., 2024](#bib.bib38)), together with broader evaluations of
research abilities ([Wan et al., 2026](#bib.bib92)). These lines of work
have made impact in mathematics ([OpenAI, 2026c](#bib.bib64); [OpenAI,
2026b](#bib.bib63); [Bubeck et al., 2025](#bib.bib7); [Woodruff et al.,
2026](#bib.bib98)), chemistry ([Yang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib101); [Boiko
et al., 2023](#bib.bib5)), materials science ([Ghafarollahi and Buehler,
2025](#bib.bib20)), earth science ([Feng et al., 2026a](#bib.bib17)),
biology ([Swanson et al., 2025](#bib.bib85); [Wang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib93); [Truhn et al., 2026](#bib.bib88); [Anthropic,
2026](#bib.bib2)), and the development of LLMs themselves ([Karpathy,
2026](#bib.bib33); [OpenAI, 2026a](#bib.bib62); [Favaro and Clark,
2026](#bib.bib16)). As generation scales up, validating the generated
hypotheses becomes the main cost ([Wallace et al., 2026](#bib.bib90)),
and ideas that look promising often degrade once executed ([Si et al.,
2026](#bib.bib79)), which motivates us to study how to reuse experience
to reduce the evaluations needed in evolutionary discovery.

Evolutionary coding agents. FunSearch ([Romera-Paredes et al.,
2024](#bib.bib71)) pairs an LLM with an evaluator and a program database
to discover new constructions in extremal combinatorics, and AlphaEvolve
([Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib61)) extends the loop to full codebases
with an ensemble of LLMs, with applications to a large set of
mathematical problems ([Georgiev et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)). Follow-up
frameworks improve the search process: OpenEvolve provides an
open-source implementation ([Sharma, 2025](#bib.bib74)); ShinkaEvolve
improves sample efficiency with parent sampling, novelty rejection,
bandit-based LLM selection, and a meta-scratchpad that summarizes
insights of recent programs ([Lange et al., 2026](#bib.bib37));
CodeEvolve and GigaEvo maintain diversity with island models and
quality-diversity archives ([Assumpção et al., 2025](#bib.bib4);
[Khrulkov et al., 2025](#bib.bib35)); MCTS-AHD organizes heuristics in a
Monte Carlo search tree ([Zheng et al., 2025b](#bib.bib114)); and
AdaEvolve adapts search intensity and resource allocation from the
history of improvements ([Cemri et al., 2026](#bib.bib8)). The paradigm
has also been applied to equation discovery ([Shojaee et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib77)) and systems research ([Cheng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib12)). SCS shows that simply conditioning on previous
solutions is competitive with more elaborate pipelines ([Gideoni et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22)), which we adopt as the backbone and main baseline.
Classical evolutionary computation also reuses experience through credit
assignment over predefined units: adaptive operator selection allocates
budget across operators with multi-armed bandits ([Da Costa et al.,
2008](#bib.bib13)), quality-diversity methods maintain elites across
behavior niches ([Mouret and Clune, 2015](#bib.bib60)) or search for
novelty alone ([Lehman and Stanley, 2011](#bib.bib39)), and MuEvo
revises the priorities of heuristic components with short-budget probing
([Lv et al., 2026](#bib.bib53)). In ExpEvolve, the units receiving
credit are ideas discovered during the search, and plateau handling
targets the ideas shared by top programs.

Learned mutators and self-improving agents. Another line trains the LLM
mutator with reinforcement learning, either during evolution ([Šurina et
al., 2025](#bib.bib84)) or at test time on a single problem ([Wang et
al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Yuksekgonul et al., 2026](#bib.bib109)), where
experience is stored in model weights. Self-improving agents such as the
Darwin Gödel Machine and the Huxley-Gödel Machine evolve the code of the
agent itself ([Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib110); [Wang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib95)), SATLUTION evolves a solver repository together with
its own rulebase ([Yu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib107)), and AlphaResearch
alternates between idea proposal and program verification ([Yu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib108)). These directions are orthogonal to ours, which
uses a fixed LLM and a fixed harness.

Causality for scientific discovery. There is a long history of
discussions on how to understand the world through observations
([Greenland et al., 1999](#bib.bib25); [Spirtes et al.,
2000](#bib.bib82); [Pearl, 2009](#bib.bib65)). One research line is
causal discovery, which learns the causal structure among variables from
observational data under assumptions such as conditional independence or
constrained functional forms ([Spirtes et al., 1995](#bib.bib81);
[Shimizu et al., 2006](#bib.bib76); [Hoyer et al., 2008](#bib.bib26)),
from interventional data and data of multiple domains ([Yang et al.,
2018](#bib.bib103); [Brouillard et al., 2020](#bib.bib6); [Mooij et al.,
2020](#bib.bib59); [Huang et al., 2020](#bib.bib27); [Perry et al.,
2022](#bib.bib67)), and in the presence of latent variables ([Li et al.,
2025d](#bib.bib45); [Li and Liu, 2025](#bib.bib44)), while experiment
design selects the interventions that make the causal structure
identifiable ([Hyttinen et al., 2013](#bib.bib30); [Li et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib40)). Recently, LLMs have been used to construct
structured variables out of unstructured data ([Liu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib47); [Li et al., 2025b](#bib.bib41)), to estimate
treatment effects from unstructured data ([Dhawan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib14)), and to propose instrumental variables ([Sheth et
al., 2025](#bib.bib75)). Compared with these works, the variables in
ExpEvolve, i.e., ideas, are constructed from unstructured programs, and
are evaluated through interventions that the search itself chooses
adaptively; Sec.
[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
characterizes what such an archive can identify.

## Appendix C A Causal View of the Formulation

In this section, we present a more detailed discussion of the causal
view of evolutionary discovery in Sec.
[3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Evolutionary Discovery as a POMDP ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").

### C.1 Formulation of Scientific Discovery

Scientific discovery aims to uncover the underlying scientific knowledge
or the causal mechanisms from interactions with the world ([Kuhn and
Hawkins, 1963](#bib.bib36)), which can be formulated as a Partially
Observed Markov Decision Process (POMDP) ([Kaelbling et al.,
1998](#bib.bib32)) (Fig.
[10](#A3.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ C.1 Formulation of Scientific Discovery ‣ Appendix C A Causal View of the Formulation ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 10: The iterative scientific discovery loop. Left: Conceptual
flow of the agent. The agent maintains a scratchpad memory ($`m`$),
proposes a program ($`p`$), and observes the outcome ($`y`$) which is
constrained by the unknown world state ($`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$). The
outcome feeds back into the memory for the next step. Right: The diagram
illustrates how the AI Scientist probes the unknown world state
$`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$. By proposing a candidate program $`p_{t}`$,
the agent triggers an experiment yielding outcome $`y_{t}`$. This
observation provides evidence about $`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$, which is
integrated into the agent’s scratchpad memory $`m_{t+1}`$. Over time
steps $`t,t+1,\dots`$, this recurrent process allows the agent to
navigate the performance landscape and converge towards optimal programs
despite the static but unknown nature of $`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$.

#### Scientific knowledge.

The primary objective of an AI Scientist is to uncover the *underlying
scientific knowledge* about the task-world, represented by a latent
variable $`\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}}\in\Theta`$, where $`\Theta`$ may encode
causal structure, mechanisms, inductive biases, constraints, etc.
Specifically, $`\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}}=\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$ can be
parameterized as a Structural Causal Model (SCM)
$`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}=(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{F},P_{U})`$ ([Spirtes et
al., 2000](#bib.bib82)), where $`\mathcal{G}=(V,E)`$ is a directed graph
whose nodes $`V`$ represent variables of interest and whose edges $`E`$
encode direct causal dependencies; $`\mathcal{F}=\{f_{v}\}_{v\in V}`$ is
a collection of structural equations $`v=f_{v}(\mathrm{Pa}(v),u_{v})`$,
where $`\mathrm{Pa}(v)`$ denotes the parents of $`v`$ in $`\mathcal{G}`$
and $`u_{v}`$ is an exogenous noise variable; $`P_{U}`$ is a
distribution over the exogenous variables $`U=\{u_{v}\}_{v\in V}`$.

#### Evaluation as intervention on SCM.

Given the SCM parametrization of $`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$, we can
consider that a program $`p\in\mathcal{P}`$ is encoded as a particular
configuration of design variables $`X=x_{p}`$. Then, $`F`$ can be
implemented as

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
F(p;\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}):=\mathbb{E}\big[\,Y\,\big|\,\mathrm{do}(X=x_{p}),\,\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}\big],
``` |  |

i.e., the expected outcome under the intervention
$`\mathrm{do}(X=x_{p})`$ in the true causal model
$`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$. Typical implementations of $`F`$ can be the
objective value of a combinatorial optimization problem, the efficiency
of a kernel program, or the performance of a machine learning model
([Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib61)).

#### Belief as revealed knowledge.

As in Sec.
[3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Evolutionary Discovery as a POMDP ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
the AI Scientist maintains a memory $`m_{t}=\Phi(h_{t})`$ as an
approximate belief about $`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$. Each evaluation step
$`(p_{t},y_{t})`$ thus updates $`m_{t}`$, which in turn updates the
agent’s effective belief about $`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$. In this sense,
each step *reveals part of the underlying scientific knowledge*, which
in turn determines the next action $`p_{t+1}`$.

### C.2 Ideas and Causal Representation Learning

#### Ideas as high-level causal variables.

In the SCM view above, a program specifies a configuration $`x_{p}`$ of
design variables $`X`$, which are low-level and high-dimensional, e.g.,
every line of the code. An idea $`z`$ (Definition
[3.2](#S3.Thmtheorem2 "Definition 3.2 (Idea). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"))
is a function of the program, and hence of $`x_{p}`$, that summarizes
the design variables at a higher level. A faithful idea representation
(Sec.
[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"))
requires that
$`\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathrm{do}(X=x_{p}),\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}]`$ depends
on $`x_{p}`$ only through $`Z(p)`$, i.e., interventions on the design
variables that keep all ideas fixed leave the expected outcome
unchanged. Hence, an intervention on the ideas is well defined at the
level of expected outcomes. This condition is related to causal feature
learning ([Chalupka et al., 2015](#bib.bib9)), which constructs
macro-level causal variables by grouping the micro-level states that
induce the same outcome distribution under intervention, and to causal
abstraction ([Rubenstein et al., 2017](#bib.bib72)), which studies when
a high-level causal model is consistent with a low-level one.
Faithfulness is a mean-level version of these conditions, restricted to
the score of interest.

#### Relation to causal representation learning.

Causal representation learning (CRL) aims to recover high-level causal
variables from low-level observations ([Schölkopf et al.,
2021](#bib.bib73)), where identifiability usually relies on additional
information such as interventions on the latent variables ([Ahuja et
al., 2023](#bib.bib1)). Ideas can be viewed as the high-level causal
variables of programs, and the two settings differ in three aspects. (i)
In CRL, the representation is usually an encoder learned from the
observations, while an idea is an interpretable function of the program
that an LLM can annotate, similar to how LLMs construct high-level
variables from unstructured data ([Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib47); [Li et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib41)). (ii) CRL usually aims to recover all latent
variables, while ideas only need to be faithful to the score. (iii) The
agent decides which programs to evaluate, and an edit that changes one
idea and keeps the others fixed acts as an intervention on that idea,
although an LLM edit may also change other ideas. Theorem
[3.3](#S3.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 3.3 (Degenerated exploration of ideas). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
shows that when the evaluated programs do not vary the candidate ideas,
the ideas that matter cannot be identified from the scores.

### C.3 Essentiality of Causal Knowledge for AI Scientists

If the evaluation revealed the scientific knowledge completely, then
with more experiment turns, the agent’s revealed scientific knowledge
would converge to $`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$. However, the observation
from the evaluation is usually only a proxy of the scientific knowledge
$`\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$: each evaluation returns a scalar score of the
program that the agent chooses to evaluate. Different hypotheses about
$`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$, e.g., ones under which different ideas
determine the score, can produce the same scores on all evaluated
programs. For example, if all evaluated programs in circle packing share
the same initialization and the same refinement, the scores cannot tell
which of the two accounts for the performance. Therefore, the causal
knowledge often cannot be identified from the scores of the programs
explored so far, and it is essential for an AI Scientist to explore
sufficiently, i.e., to evaluate programs that distinguish the competing
hypotheses. We denote by $`e_{\mathrm{src}}`$ the environment in which
the evaluation is conducted.

###### Definition C.1 (Causal AI Scientist).

A *Causal AI Scientist* is an agent specified by: (i) a policy
$`\pi_{t}(\cdot\mid\theta_{t},e_{\mathrm{src}})`$ selecting $`p_{t}`$,
(ii) a counterfactual / explanatory operator $`\mathrm{CF}`$, that
answer interventional queries $`(e,p)`$ via
$`\mathrm{CF}(\theta_{t};e,p)`$ as an “explanation” of predicted
performance, where $`\theta_{t}`$ is the knowledge revealed at turn
$`t`$.

Without the revealing of the causal knowledge, the discovery process
suffers from significant inefficiency and suboptimality issues. We
discuss the two issues more concretely below.

Evolutionary efficiency of Causal AI Scientist. The efficiency issue is
characterized by Theorem
[3.1](#S3.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 3.1 (Structured experience reuse, informal). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").
In the linear setting of Theorem
[3.1](#S3.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 3.1 (Structured experience reuse, informal). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
a Causal AI Scientist can be implemented via estimating the
$`w^{\star}`$ and optimizing for $`\hat{p}`$ from the history, while the
black-box baseline does not consider the interactions between the
historical observations. Theorem
[3.1](#S3.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 3.1 (Structured experience reuse, informal). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
shows that, when $`K\gg d`$, which is usually the case as the space for
all programs is significantly larger than the underlying SCM, encoding
(correct) causal structure, e.g., a faithful idea representation, yields
an exponential (or at least multiplicative) gain in sample efficiency
under finite budgets. For example, if $`K`$ grows exponentially with
$`d`$, e.g., $`K=2^{d}`$, the upper bound in Theorem
[3.1](#S3.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 3.1 (Structured experience reuse, informal). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
grows polynomially in $`d`$, as
$`O\big(d\,(d+\log\frac{1}{\delta})\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\big)`$,
while the lower bound for the black-box baseline grows exponentially in
$`d`$, as
$`\Omega\big(2^{d}\log\frac{1}{\delta}\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\big)`$.

Sufficient exploration of Causal AI Scientist. The suboptimality issue
is characterized by Theorem
[3.3](#S3.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 3.3 (Degenerated exploration of ideas). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").
Let $`S\subseteq\mathcal{P}`$ be the set of programs evaluated by the
agent. Two hypotheses $`\theta_{0}`$ and $`\theta_{1}`$ can be
distinguished from the history only if their observation models differ
on some program in $`S`$; otherwise, the history has the same
distribution under both hypotheses. Under the idea-level mechanisms in
Theorem
[3.3](#S3.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 3.3 (Degenerated exploration of ideas). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
i.e., $`F(p;\theta_{i})=g(Z(p),z_{i}(p))`$ for $`i\in\{0,1\}`$, the two
hypotheses agree on every program where $`z_{0}`$ and $`z_{1}`$ agree,
so only the programs where the two ideas differ can distinguish them.
Intuitively, Theorem
[3.3](#S3.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 3.3 (Degenerated exploration of ideas). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
implies that if the evaluated programs do not distinguish the
corresponding $`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$ among
$`\{\theta_{0},\theta_{1}\}`$, then the solution $`\hat{p}`$ incurs an
expected regret of at least $`\Delta/2`$ under one of them, regardless
of the budget. This situation is common in evolutionary search: as the
search concentrates around its current best programs, the ideas shared
by these programs stop varying among the evaluated programs, and the
scores cannot tell whether these ideas are the ones that matter. Hence,
a Causal AI Scientist needs to explore the programs in which the
competing ideas differ, so that the scores can distinguish the
hypotheses. This barrier can be removed by exploration within the same
evaluator, which differs from the transfer across environments discussed
below.

### C.4 Transfer of Scientific Knowledge across Environments

Beyond a single evaluator, the revealed scientific knowledge is also
expected to transfer to other environments. If the objective function
$`F`$ is static universally, then with more experiment turns, the
optimized solution $`p_{t}`$ and the agent’s revealed scientific
knowledge can also be applied universally. However, the evaluation is
usually conducted at some specific environment $`e\in\mathcal{E}`$,
which only gives a proxy knowledge $`\theta_{e}`$ about the scientific
knowledge $`\Theta_{\text{sci}}`$. For example, the performance of a
machine learning model is usually assessed on finite samples from the
test distribution, and there also exist distribution shifts from the
test distribution when deploying the model in the real world
([Quinonero-Candela et al., 2008](#bib.bib69)). Different from
$`\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$ that characterizes the complete causal
structure about the scientific problem, optimization under environment
$`\theta_{e}`$ may introduce some spurious correlations that maximize
the objective value $`F_{e}`$ ([Chen et al., 2023](#bib.bib11)).
Therefore, to retain the optimality of $`\hat{p}`$ beyond the source
environment $`e_{\mathrm{src}}`$ to some target $`e_{\mathrm{tgt}}`$, it
is essential to reveal the causal knowledge and answer causal questions
for an AI Scientist, e.g., through the operator $`\mathrm{CF}`$ in
Definition
[C.1](#A3.Thmtheorem1 "Definition C.1 (Causal AI Scientist). ‣ C.3 Essentiality of Causal Knowledge for AI Scientists ‣ Appendix C A Causal View of the Formulation ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").
Let $`P_{e}(\cdot\mid p,\theta)`$ denote the observation model of the
evaluator in environment $`e`$, with mean $`F_{e}(p;\theta)`$. We have
the following:

###### Theorem C.2.

Consider $`e_{\mathrm{src}},e_{\mathrm{tgt}}\in\mathcal{E}`$ and
$`\theta_{0},\theta_{1}\in\Theta`$ such that
$`P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(\cdot\mid p,\theta_{0})=P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(\cdot\mid p,\theta_{1})`$
for all $`p\in\mathcal{P}`$, and the optimal programs in
$`e_{\mathrm{tgt}}`$ under $`\theta_{0}`$ and $`\theta_{1}`$ are
different and unique, each better than all other programs by at least
$`\Delta>0`$. Then for any policy $`\pi`$ that can interact only with
$`e_{\mathrm{src}}`$, there exists $`i\in\{0,1\}`$ such that for every
budget $`T`$,
$`\mathbb{E}\big[\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p;\theta_{i})-F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(\hat{p};\theta_{i})\big]\geq\Delta/2`$.

The formal description and the proof are given in Appendix
[G](#A7 "Appendix G Proof of Theorem (Non-identifiability under environment shifts) ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").
Intuitively, Theorem
[C.2](#A3.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem C.2. ‣ C.4 Transfer of Scientific Knowledge across Environments ‣ Appendix C A Causal View of the Formulation ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
implies that if the source environment does not distinguish the
corresponding $`\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$ among
$`\{\theta_{0},\theta_{1}\}`$, then the solution $`\hat{p}`$ solved
given source environment is suboptimal in the target environment under
one of them, no matter how many evaluations are made in the source
environment. In the real world, it is usually the case that two machine
learning models will have similar performances under the public test
benchmarks, but exhibit significantly different behaviors when
generalizing to distributions from other environments. Different from
Theorem
[3.3](#S3.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 3.3 (Degenerated exploration of ideas). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
this barrier cannot be removed by more exploration in the source
environment, since the two hypotheses agree on every program there. We
leave a full study of the transfer of scientific knowledge across
environments to future work.

## Appendix D Additional Technical Details

### D.1 Notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|----|----|
| $`\mathcal{P}`$ | Program / pipeline / model space (candidate designs) |
| $`K`$ | Number of candidate programs, $`K:=|\mathcal{P}|`$ (finite in Theorem [3.1](#S3.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 3.1 (Structured experience reuse, informal). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")) |
| $`p\in\mathcal{P}`$ | A program to evaluate (action) |
| $`\mathcal{X}`$ | Design-variable space (encoding of programs) |
| $`x_{p}\in\mathcal{X}`$ | Encoding of program $`p`$ (e.g., design variables $`X=x_{p}`$) |
| $`z`$, $`Z(p)`$ | An idea and the idea representation of program $`p`$ (Definition [3.2](#S3.Thmtheorem2 "Definition 3.2 (Idea). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")) |
| $`r`$ | Number of ideas in an idea representation |
| $`\phi(p)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}`$ | Known representation of program $`p`$ in Theorem [3.1](#S3.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 3.1 (Structured experience reuse, informal). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"), e.g., the one-hot encoding of $`Z(p)`$ |
| $`d`$ | Dimension of the representation, e.g., the number of value combinations of the ideas |
| $`\Theta`$ | Hypothesis space of scientific knowledge (e.g., SCMs / mechanisms) |
| $`\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$ | Latent RV taking values in $`\Theta`$ (Bayesian view) |
| $`\theta^{\star}\in\Theta`$ | True (fixed but unknown) scientific knowledge instance (realization) |
| $`\mu_{0}`$ | Prior over $`\Theta`$ (i.e., $`\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}}\sim\mu_{0}`$) |
| $`\mathcal{E}`$ | Environment / protocol index set (evaluation regimes, deployments) |
| $`e\in\mathcal{E}`$ | Environment index; $`e_{\mathrm{src}}`$ source, $`e_{\mathrm{tgt}}`$ target |
| $`F_{e}(p;\theta)`$ | True performance in env $`e`$ (scalar objective) |
| $`P_{e}(\cdot\mid p,\theta)`$ | Observation model (likelihood) for evaluator output in env $`e`$ |
| $`y_{t}`$ | Observed evaluator outcome at round $`t`$ |
| $`h_{t}`$ | History $`\{(p_{0},y_{0}),\dots,(p_{t-1},y_{t-1})\}`$ |
| $`b_{t}`$ | Bayesian belief/posterior over $`\theta`$: $`b_{t}(\cdot)=\Pr(\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}}\in\cdot\mid h_{t},e_{\mathrm{src}})`$ |
| $`T`$ | Evaluation budget / horizon (number of program evaluations) |

Table 2: Notation used in the formulation and theorems.

### D.2 Random variable, space, and realization (to avoid notation confusion)

We use the following (standard) convention.

(i) Hypothesis space. $`\Theta`$ is a set that contains all candidate
scientific-knowledge hypotheses.

(ii) True but unknown instance. The real world is governed by a fixed
but unknown $`\theta^{\star}\in\Theta`$.

(iii) Bayesian view (optional but convenient). A Bayesian agent models
uncertainty by treating $`\theta^{\star}`$ as a realization of a latent
random variable $`\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$ with prior $`\mu_{0}`$, i.e.
$`\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}}\sim\mu_{0}`$ and $`\theta^{\star}`$ is one draw
from it. The belief $`b_{t}`$ is simply the posterior distribution of
$`\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}}`$ after seeing history $`h_{t}`$.

(iv) Does scientific knowledge change across environments? In our
formulation, the *underlying* scientific knowledge $`\theta^{\star}`$ is
static across rounds. Different environments $`e\in\mathcal{E}`$
represent different evaluation/deployment protocols (distribution
shifts, constraint changes, measurement noise, private vs public tests,
etc.). Formally, environments affect either the true performance map
$`F_{e}(\cdot;\theta)`$ and/or the observation kernel
$`P_{e}(\cdot\mid p,\theta)`$, while $`\theta^{\star}`$ itself remains
the same hidden instance.

### D.3 Evaluator as an observation model (covers deterministic and stochastic evaluators)

Fix an environment $`e\in\mathcal{E}`$. When the agent evaluates program
$`p`$, it receives an observation $`y\in\mathcal{Y}`$ drawn from

|     |                                          |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       y\sim P_{e}(\cdot\mid p,\theta^{\star}),
       ```                                       |     |

where $`P_{e}(\cdot\mid p,\theta)`$ is a conditional distribution on
$`\mathcal{Y}`$.

#### Deterministic evaluator.

A deterministic evaluator is the special case where there exists a
function $`g_{e}`$ such that

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
P_{e}(\cdot\mid p,\theta)=\delta_{g_{e}(p;\theta)}(\cdot),\quad\text{i.e.,}\quad y=g_{e}(p;\theta^{\star})\ \text{a.s.}
``` |  |

In many program-evolution settings, the evaluator is designed to
deterministically check validity and compute an objective score (e.g.,
via a verifier and a scoring routine).

#### Stochastic/noisy evaluator.

A common instantiation is additive noise:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
y=F_{e}(p;\theta^{\star})+\varepsilon,\qquad\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}),
``` |  |

but only the proof of Theorem
[3.1](#S3.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 3.1 (Structured experience reuse, informal). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
relies on the Gaussian form; the other results hold for any noise
distribution shared by the hypotheses.

### D.4 Belief and Bayes update: kernel form and undergraduate-friendly special cases

Let $`h_{t}=\{(p_{0},y_{0}),\dots,(p_{t-1},y_{t-1})\}`$ be the history.
The Bayesian belief (posterior) is

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
b_{t}(B)=\Pr(\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}}\in B\mid h_{t},e_{\mathrm{src}}),\qquad B\subseteq\Theta.
``` |  |

#### General Bayes update (kernel form).

After choosing $`p_{t}`$ and observing $`y_{t}`$ in
$`e_{\mathrm{src}}`$, the posterior is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
b_{t+1}(B)=\frac{\int_{B}P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(dy_{t}\mid p_{t},\theta)\,b_{t}(d\theta)}{\int_{\Theta}P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(dy_{t}\mid p_{t},\theta)\,b_{t}(d\theta)}.
``` |  | (2) |

#### Finite hypothesis space (sum form).

If $`\Theta=\{\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{N}\}`$ is finite and the
likelihood has a pmf
$`P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(y_{t}\mid p_{t},\theta_{i})`$, then

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
b_{t+1}(\theta_{i})=\frac{b_{t}(\theta_{i})\,P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(y_{t}\mid p_{t},\theta_{i})}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}b_{t}(\theta_{j})\,P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(y_{t}\mid p_{t},\theta_{j})}.
``` |  |

#### Continuous hypothesis space (density form).

If $`P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(dy\mid p,\theta)`$ has a density
$`p_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(y\mid p,\theta)`$, then

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
b_{t+1}(\theta)=\frac{b_{t}(\theta)\,p_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(y_{t}\mid p_{t},\theta)}{\int_{\Theta}b_{t}(\theta^{\prime})\,p_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(y_{t}\mid p_{t},\theta^{\prime})\,d\theta^{\prime}}.
``` |  |

#### Deterministic evaluator (indicator/filter form).

If $`y=g_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(p;\theta)`$ deterministically, then the
update becomes

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
b_{t+1}(d\theta)\ \propto\ \mathbf{1}\{g_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(p_{t};\theta)=y_{t}\}\,b_{t}(d\theta),
``` |  |

i.e. the posterior is the prior restricted to hypotheses consistent with
the observed outcome.

## Appendix E Proof of Theorem [3.1](#S3.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 3.1 (Structured experience reuse, informal). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery") (Structured experience reuse)

Throughout this section we fix a *single* static environment (drop $`e`$
from notation), and assume $`\mathcal{P}=\{p_{1},\dots,p_{K}\}`$ is
finite.

### E.1 Protocol and performance criterion

#### Experiment–then–commit protocol.

A policy $`\pi`$ interacts for $`T`$ rounds. At each round
$`t=0,\dots,T-1`$ it selects a program $`p_{t}\in\mathcal{P}`$ (possibly
randomized) based on the past history $`h_{t}`$, then observes
$`y_{t}\in\mathbb{R}`$. After $`T`$ evaluations it outputs a final
recommendation $`\hat{p}\in\mathcal{P}`$.

#### Simple regret.

Let $`f(p)`$ denote the true mean performance of program $`p`$ in this
environment. Define the (random) simple regret

|     |                                                             |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathrm{SR}_{T}:=\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}f(p)\;-\;f(\hat{p}).
       ```                                                          |     | (3) |

#### $`(\epsilon,\delta)`$-correctness (uniform).

Fix $`\epsilon>0`$ and $`\delta\in(0,1)`$. We say a policy $`\pi`$ is
*$`(\epsilon,\delta)`$-correct uniformly on a hypothesis class
$`\mathcal{H}`$* if for every instance in $`\mathcal{H}`$,

|     |                                                        |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \Pr\big(\mathrm{SR}_{T}\leq\epsilon\big)\geq 1-\delta.
       ```                                                     |     |

“Uniformly” means the guarantee must hold for *all* instances in the
class, not only on average.

### E.2 Two hypothesis classes

(1) Structured class. Each program $`p`$ has a known representation
$`\phi(p)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}`$ with $`\|\phi(p)\|_{2}\leq 1`$, e.g., a
faithful linear idea representation $`\phi(p)=Z(p)`$ (Sec.
[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")).
The unknown instance is a weight vector $`w^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}`$
and

|     |                                       |     |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       f(p)=\langle\phi(p),w^{\star}\rangle.
       ```                                    |     | (4) |

Observations follow a Gaussian noise model

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
y_{t}=f(p_{t})+\varepsilon_{t},\qquad\varepsilon_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})\ \text{i.i.d.}
``` |  | (5) |

*Coverage condition.* Assume there exist $`d`$ basis programs
$`p^{(1)},\dots,p^{(d)}`$ whose representations are the standard basis:

|     |                                         |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \phi(p^{(i)})=e_{i},\qquad i=1,\dots,d.
       ```                                      |     | (6) |

(2) Unstructured black-box class (baseline). The unknown instance is an
arbitrary vector of means

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mu=(\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{K})\in\mathbb{R}^{K},\qquad f(p_{i})=\mu_{i},
``` |  |

and observations are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
y_{t}=\mu_{I_{t}}+\varepsilon_{t},\qquad\varepsilon_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})\ \text{i.i.d.},
``` |  | (7) |

where $`I_{t}\in\{1,\dots,K\}`$ is the index of the chosen program
$`p_{t}=p_{I_{t}}`$. Crucially, there is *no assumed relation* between
$`\mu_{i}`$ and $`\mu_{j}`$ for $`i\neq j`$.

### E.3 Formal statement and proof

###### Theorem E.1 (Formal version of Theorem [3.1](#S3.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 3.1 (Structured experience reuse, informal). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")).

Fix $`\epsilon>0`$ and $`\delta\in(0,1/4)`$.

1.  1.
    (Upper bound under the structured linear class). Under equation
    [4](#A5.E4 "In E.2 Two hypothesis classes ‣ Appendix E Proof of Theorem (Structured experience reuse) ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")–equation
    [6](#A5.E6 "In E.2 Two hypothesis classes ‣ Appendix E Proof of Theorem (Structured experience reuse) ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
    and equation
    [5](#A5.E5 "In E.2 Two hypothesis classes ‣ Appendix E Proof of Theorem (Structured experience reuse) ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
    there exists a policy $`\pi_{\mathrm{lin}}`$ such that

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \Pr\big(\mathrm{SR}_{T}\leq 2\epsilon\big)\geq 1-\delta\quad\text{whenever}\quad T\ \geq\ 2d\,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\log\!\Big(\frac{2K}{\delta}\Big).
    ``` |  |
2.  2.
    (Lower bound for the unstructured black-box class). For the
    black-box class equation
    [7](#A5.E7 "In E.2 Two hypothesis classes ‣ Appendix E Proof of Theorem (Structured experience reuse) ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
    any policy that is $`(\epsilon,\delta)`$-correct *uniformly for all*
    $`\mu\in\mathbb{R}^{K}`$ must satisfy

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    T\ \geq\ (K-1)\,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{8\epsilon^{2}}\,\log\!\Big(\frac{1}{2\delta}\Big).
    ``` |  |

Replacing $`\epsilon`$ with $`\epsilon/2`$ in part (1) gives the
informal statement in Theorem
[3.1](#S3.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 3.1 (Structured experience reuse, informal). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").

###### Proof.

We prove the two parts separately.

#### Part (1): constructive upper bound (estimate $`w^{\star}`$ then commit).

Evaluate each basis program $`p^{(i)}`$ exactly $`n`$ times (total
$`T=nd`$). Let $`y^{(i)}_{1},\dots,y^{(i)}_{n}`$ be the observations for
basis $`i`$, and define

|     |                                                    |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \hat{w}_{i}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}y^{(i)}_{j}.
       ```                                                 |     |

By equation
[4](#A5.E4 "In E.2 Two hypothesis classes ‣ Appendix E Proof of Theorem (Structured experience reuse) ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")–equation
[6](#A5.E6 "In E.2 Two hypothesis classes ‣ Appendix E Proof of Theorem (Structured experience reuse) ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
$`f(p^{(i)})=w^{\star}_{i}`$. By equation
[5](#A5.E5 "In E.2 Two hypothesis classes ‣ Appendix E Proof of Theorem (Structured experience reuse) ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
$`\hat{w}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(w^{\star}_{i},\sigma^{2}/n)`$ and these
coordinates are independent.

Define for any program $`p`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widehat{f}(p):=\langle\phi(p),\hat{w}\rangle,\qquad\hat{w}=(\hat{w}_{1},\dots,\hat{w}_{d}).
``` |  |

Then

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widehat{f}(p)-f(p)=\langle\phi(p),\hat{w}-w^{\star}\rangle\sim\mathcal{N}\!\Big(0,\ \frac{\sigma^{2}}{n}\|\phi(p)\|_{2}^{2}\Big),
``` |  |

so since $`\|\phi(p)\|_{2}\leq 1`$,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Pr\big(|\widehat{f}(p)-f(p)|\geq\epsilon\big)\leq 2\exp\!\Big(-\frac{n\epsilon^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\Big).
``` |  |

Union bound over $`K`$ programs gives

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Pr\Big(\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}|\widehat{f}(p)-f(p)|\geq\epsilon\Big)\leq 2K\exp\!\Big(-\frac{n\epsilon^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\Big).
``` |  |

Choose

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
n\ \geq\ 2\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\log\!\Big(\frac{2K}{\delta}\Big),
``` |  |

so that with probability at least $`1-\delta`$ we have
$`\max_{p}|\widehat{f}(p)-f(p)|\leq\epsilon`$.

Now output $`\hat{p}:=\arg\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\widehat{f}(p)`$. Let
$`p^{\star}:=\arg\max_{p}f(p)`$. On the above high-probability event,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
f(p^{\star})-f(\hat{p})\leq\big(f(p^{\star})-\widehat{f}(p^{\star})\big)+\big(\widehat{f}(\hat{p})-f(\hat{p})\big)\leq\epsilon+\epsilon=2\epsilon.
``` |  |

Thus $`\Pr(\mathrm{SR}_{T}\leq 2\epsilon)\geq 1-\delta`$ for $`T=nd`$ as
stated.

#### Part (2): lower bound for the black-box class.

We construct $`K`$ hard instances and lower bound any uniformly
$`(\epsilon,\delta)`$-correct policy.

Let the programs be $`p_{1},\dots,p_{K}`$. Define a base instance
$`\mu^{(0)}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}`$:

|     |                                                                  |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mu^{(0)}_{1}=0,\qquad\mu^{(0)}_{i}=-2\epsilon\ \ (i=2,\dots,K).
       ```                                                               |     |

For each $`i\in\{2,\dots,K\}`$, define an alternative instance
$`\mu^{(i)}`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mu^{(i)}_{1}=0,\qquad\mu^{(i)}_{i}=+2\epsilon,\qquad\mu^{(i)}_{j}=-2\epsilon\ \ (j\notin\{1,i\}).
``` |  |

Under $`\mu^{(0)}`$, the unique best program is $`p_{1}`$, and choosing
any $`p_{i}`$ with $`i\geq 2`$ incurs regret $`2\epsilon>\epsilon`$.
Under $`\mu^{(i)}`$, the unique best program is $`p_{i}`$, and choosing
$`p_{1}`$ incurs regret $`2\epsilon>\epsilon`$.

Let $`P_{0}`$ be the distribution of the full transcript
$`\mathcal{T}:=(p_{0:T-1},y_{0:T-1},\hat{p})`$ under $`\mu^{(0)}`$, and
$`P_{i}`$ the analogous distribution under $`\mu^{(i)}`$. Uniform
$`(\epsilon,\delta)`$-correctness implies

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
P_{0}(\hat{p}=p_{1})\geq 1-\delta,\qquad P_{i}(\hat{p}=p_{1})\leq\delta\quad(i=2,\dots,K).
``` |  |

Step 1: a KL lower bound from an event. For any event $`A`$ and
distributions $`P,Q`$, one has

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)\geq P(A)\log\frac{P(A)}{Q(A)}+(1-P(A))\log\frac{1-P(A)}{1-Q(A)}.
``` |  |

Apply it with $`A=\{\hat{p}=p_{1}\}`$, $`P=P_{0}`$, $`Q=P_{i}`$. Let
$`p:=P_{0}(A)\geq 1-\delta`$ and $`q:=P_{i}(A)\leq\delta`$. For
$`\delta\in(0,1/4)`$ this yields

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{KL}(P_{0}\|P_{i})\ \geq\ \log\!\Big(\frac{1}{2\delta}\Big).
``` |  | (8) |

Step 2: compute $`\mathrm{KL}(P_{0}\|P_{i})`$ via number of pulls of arm
$`i`$. Under $`\mu^{(0)}`$ and $`\mu^{(i)}`$, the policy is identical;
only observations when playing $`p_{i}`$ differ:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
y\sim\mathcal{N}(-2\epsilon,\sigma^{2})\ \text{under }\mu^{(0)},\qquad y\sim\mathcal{N}(+2\epsilon,\sigma^{2})\ \text{under }\mu^{(i)}.
``` |  |

For Gaussians with equal variance,
$`\mathrm{KL}(\mathcal{N}(m_{0},\sigma^{2})\|\mathcal{N}(m_{1},\sigma^{2}))=\frac{(m_{0}-m_{1})^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}`$,
so each pull of $`p_{i}`$ contributes KL
$`\frac{(4\epsilon)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}=\frac{8\epsilon^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}`$.

Let $`N_{i}`$ be the (random) number of times $`p_{i}`$ is evaluated in
$`T`$ rounds. Additivity of log-likelihood ratios over independent
Gaussian samples yields

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{KL}(P_{0}\|P_{i})=\frac{8\epsilon^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\ \mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[N_{i}].
``` |  | (9) |

Step 3: conclude the lower bound on $`T`$. Combine equation
[8](#A5.E8 "In Part (2): lower bound for the black-box class. ‣ E.3 Formal statement and proof ‣ Appendix E Proof of Theorem (Structured experience reuse) ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
and equation
[9](#A5.E9 "In Part (2): lower bound for the black-box class. ‣ E.3 Formal statement and proof ‣ Appendix E Proof of Theorem (Structured experience reuse) ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"):

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[N_{i}]\ \geq\ \frac{\sigma^{2}}{8\epsilon^{2}}\log\!\Big(\frac{1}{2\delta}\Big),\qquad i=2,\dots,K.
``` |  |

Summing over $`i=2,\dots,K`$ gives

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
T=\sum_{i=1}^{K}N_{i}\ \geq\ \sum_{i=2}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[N_{i}]\ \geq\ (K-1)\frac{\sigma^{2}}{8\epsilon^{2}}\log\!\Big(\frac{1}{2\delta}\Big).
``` |  |

This completes the proof. ∎

#### Remark (deterministic evaluator).

If $`\sigma=0`$, the structured linear class can recover $`w^{\star}`$
exactly from $`d`$ basis evaluations and achieve $`\mathrm{SR}_{T}=0`$,
while in the unstructured black-box class a uniform worst-case guarantee
requires evaluating all $`K`$ programs at least once.

#### Relation to best-arm identification.

The lower bound follows the standard change-of-measure argument for
best-arm identification in $`K`$-armed Gaussian bandits ([Kaufmann et
al., 2016](#bib.bib34)), and the upper bound is a simple instance of
best-arm identification in linear bandits ([Soare et al.,
2014](#bib.bib80)).

## Appendix F Proof of Theorem [3.3](#S3.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 3.3 (Degenerated exploration of ideas). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery") (Degenerated exploration of ideas)

### F.1 Formal statement and proof

For a policy that interacts for $`T`$ rounds and outputs $`\hat{p}`$,
define the simple regret under mechanism $`\theta`$ as
$`\mathrm{SR}_{T}(\theta)\coloneqq\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}F(p;\theta)-F(\hat{p};\theta)`$.

###### Theorem F.1 (Formal version of Theorem [3.3](#S3.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 3.3 (Degenerated exploration of ideas). ‣ 3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas ‣ 3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")).

Let $`z_{0},z_{1}:\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{V}`$ be two ideas, and let
$`A\coloneqq\{p\in\mathcal{P}:z_{0}(p)=z_{1}(p)\}`$ be the set of
programs on which they agree. Assume there exist
$`\theta_{0},\theta_{1}\in\Theta`$ such that:

1.  (i)
    (Idea-level mechanisms) $`F(p;\theta_{i})=g(Z(p),z_{i}(p))`$ for all
    $`p\in\mathcal{P}`$ and $`i\in\{0,1\}`$, for a common representation
    $`Z`$ and function $`g`$, and each evaluation returns
    $`y=F(p;\theta_{i})+\varepsilon`$ with the same noise distribution
    under $`\theta_{0}`$ and $`\theta_{1}`$;
2.  (ii)
    (Optimal program flips with margin $`\Delta`$) there exist
    $`p_{0}\neq p_{1}`$ and $`\Delta>0`$ such that
    $`F(p_{i};\theta_{i})-F(p;\theta_{i})\geq\Delta`$ for all
    $`p\neq p_{i}`$ and $`i\in\{0,1\}`$.

Then for any policy that only evaluates programs in $`A`$, there exists
$`i\in\{0,1\}`$ such that for every budget $`T`$,

|     |                                                                  |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathbb{E}\big[\mathrm{SR}_{T}(\theta_{i})\big]\ \geq\ \Delta/2.
       ```                                                               |     |

Moreover, at least one of $`p_{0}`$ and $`p_{1}`$ lies outside $`A`$.

###### Proof.

For every $`p\in A`$, $`z_{0}(p)=z_{1}(p)`$ gives
$`F(p;\theta_{0})=g(Z(p),z_{0}(p))=g(Z(p),z_{1}(p))=F(p;\theta_{1})`$.
Together with the common noise distribution in (i), the observation
model $`O(\cdot\mid\theta_{i},p)`$ is identical under $`\theta_{0}`$ and
$`\theta_{1}`$ for every $`p\in A`$.

Let $`\mathbb{P}_{i}`$ be the distribution of the transcript
$`(p_{0:T-1},y_{0:T-1},\hat{p})`$ when the true mechanism is
$`\theta_{i}`$. Since the policy only evaluates programs in $`A`$, for
any history and any chosen $`p_{t}\in A`$, the conditional distribution
of $`y_{t}`$ is identical under $`\theta_{0}`$ and $`\theta_{1}`$, and
the policy chooses $`p_{t+1}`$ and $`\hat{p}`$ with the same
randomization given the same history. By induction on $`t`$,
$`\mathbb{P}_{0}=\mathbb{P}_{1}`$. In particular, the output $`\hat{p}`$
has the same distribution $`Q`$ on $`\mathcal{P}`$ under both
mechanisms.

By (ii), any output $`\hat{p}\neq p_{i}`$ incurs regret at least
$`\Delta`$ under $`\theta_{i}`$, so

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{SR}_{T}(\theta_{0})]\ \geq\ \Delta\,\big(1-Q(\hat{p}=p_{0})\big),\qquad\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{SR}_{T}(\theta_{1})]\ \geq\ \Delta\,\big(1-Q(\hat{p}=p_{1})\big).
``` |  |

Since $`p_{0}\neq p_{1}`$, $`Q(\hat{p}=p_{0})+Q(\hat{p}=p_{1})\leq 1`$,
so at least one of the two probabilities is at most $`1/2`$, and the
corresponding expected regret is at least $`\Delta/2`$.

For the last claim, suppose both $`p_{0},p_{1}\in A`$. Then
$`F(p_{1};\theta_{0})=F(p_{1};\theta_{1})\geq F(p_{0};\theta_{1})+\Delta=F(p_{0};\theta_{0})+\Delta`$,
which contradicts the optimality of $`p_{0}`$ under $`\theta_{0}`$. ∎

The theorem holds for any budget, since the barrier comes from the
programs that the policy evaluates. To identify which of $`z_{0}`$ and
$`z_{1}`$ matters, the policy has to evaluate a program outside $`A`$,
i.e., a program on which the two ideas differ. In ExpEvolve, this is the
role of plateau-aware revision, which changes the proposal distribution
to evaluate programs where the ideas shared by the leading programs
differ.

## Appendix G Proof of Theorem [C.2](#A3.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem C.2. ‣ C.4 Transfer of Scientific Knowledge across Environments ‣ Appendix C A Causal View of the Formulation ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery") (Non-identifiability under environment shifts)

### G.1 Setup: source interaction, target evaluation, and target regret

The agent can only interact with the *source* environment
$`e_{\mathrm{src}}`$:

|     |                                                                 |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       y_{t}\sim P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(\cdot\mid p_{t},\theta^{\star}).
       ```                                                              |     |

After $`T`$ rounds it outputs a final program $`\hat{p}`$. Performance
is judged in a *target* environment $`e_{\mathrm{tgt}}`$ via
$`F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p;\theta^{\star})`$. Define the target (simple)
regret:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{GR}_{T}(\theta^{\star}):=\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p;\theta^{\star})-F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(\hat{p};\theta^{\star}).
``` |  |

### G.2 Formal statement and proof

###### Theorem G.1 (Non-identifiability barrier under shifts).

Fix $`e_{\mathrm{src}},e_{\mathrm{tgt}}\in\mathcal{E}`$. Assume there
exist two hypotheses $`\theta_{0},\theta_{1}\in\Theta`$ such that:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\textbf{(Source indistinguishability)}\quad P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(\cdot\mid p,\theta_{0})=P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(\cdot\mid p,\theta_{1}),\quad\forall p\in\mathcal{P}.`$ |  | (10) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\textbf{(Target optimal action flips with margin $\Delta$)}\quad\exists\,p_{0},p_{1}\in\mathcal{P}\ \text{and}\ \Delta>0\ \text{s.t.}`$ |  | (11) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\qquad p_{0}\in\arg\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p;\theta_{0}),\quad p_{1}\in\arg\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p;\theta_{1}),`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\qquad F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p_{0};\theta_{0})-F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p;\theta_{0})\geq\Delta,\ \forall p\neq p_{0},\quad F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p_{1};\theta_{1})-F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p;\theta_{1})\geq\Delta,\ \forall p\neq p_{1}.`$ |  | (12) |

Then for any policy $`\pi`$ that can interact only with
$`e_{\mathrm{src}}`$, there exists $`i\in\{0,1\}`$ such that for every
budget $`T`$,

|     |                                                                  |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathbb{E}\big[\mathrm{GR}_{T}(\theta_{i})\big]\ \geq\ \Delta/2.
       ```                                                               |     |

This impossibility holds whether the evaluator is stochastic or
deterministic, since equation
[10](#A7.E10 "In Theorem G.1 (Non-identifiability barrier under shifts). ‣ G.2 Formal statement and proof ‣ Appendix G Proof of Theorem (Non-identifiability under environment shifts) ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
is stated at the level of the full observation model
$`P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}`$.

###### Proof.

Let $`\mathbb{P}_{i}`$ be the distribution over the full transcript

|     |                                            |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathcal{T}:=(p_{0:T-1},y_{0:T-1},\hat{p})
       ```                                         |     |

when the true hypothesis is $`\theta_{i}`$ and interaction is only with
$`e_{\mathrm{src}}`$.

By equation
[10](#A7.E10 "In Theorem G.1 (Non-identifiability barrier under shifts). ‣ G.2 Formal statement and proof ‣ Appendix G Proof of Theorem (Non-identifiability under environment shifts) ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
for any history and any chosen action $`p_{t}`$, the conditional
distribution of $`y_{t}`$ is identical under $`\theta_{0}`$ and
$`\theta_{1}`$. By induction on $`t`$, the entire transcript
distribution is identical:

|     |                                |     |
|-----|--------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathbb{P}_{0}=\mathbb{P}_{1}.
       ```                             |     |

In particular, the marginal distribution of the final output $`\hat{p}`$
is the same under $`\theta_{0}`$ and $`\theta_{1}`$. Let this common
distribution be denoted by $`Q`$ on $`\mathcal{P}`$.

Now consider the expected target regret under $`\theta_{0}`$: by
equation
[12](#A7.E12 "In Theorem G.1 (Non-identifiability barrier under shifts). ‣ G.2 Formal statement and proof ‣ Appendix G Proof of Theorem (Non-identifiability under environment shifts) ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
any output $`\hat{p}\neq p_{0}`$ incurs regret at least $`\Delta`$ under
$`\theta_{0}`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{GR}_{T}(\theta_{0})=F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p_{0};\theta_{0})-F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(\hat{p};\theta_{0})\ \geq\ \Delta\cdot\mathbf{1}\{\hat{p}\neq p_{0}\}.
``` |  |

Taking expectation w.r.t. $`Q`$ yields

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{GR}_{T}(\theta_{0})]\ \geq\ \Delta\cdot(1-Q(\hat{p}=p_{0})).
``` |  |

Similarly,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{GR}_{T}(\theta_{1})]\ \geq\ \Delta\cdot(1-Q(\hat{p}=p_{1})).
``` |  |

Since $`Q(\hat{p}=p_{0})+Q(\hat{p}=p_{1})\leq 1`$, at least one of these
probabilities is at most $`1/2`$, so at least one of the two expected
regrets is at least $`\Delta/2`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\max\{\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{GR}_{T}(\theta_{0})],\ \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{GR}_{T}(\theta_{1})]\}\ \geq\ \Delta/2.
``` |  |

This proves the claim. ∎

### G.3 Concrete examples satisfying the conditions

We give two illustrative examples where source data cannot distinguish
two hypotheses, yet the target-optimal decision differs.

#### Example 1: public test vs private (distribution shift / shortcut feature).

Let $`\theta\in\{\theta_{0},\theta_{1}\}`$ encode which feature is truly
stable/causal. Programs correspond to two model families: $`p_{0}`$ uses
a stable causal feature; $`p_{1}`$ uses a shortcut feature. In the
source environment (public benchmark), the shortcut feature is perfectly
correlated with labels, so both hypotheses yield the same evaluator
distribution for every program, satisfying equation
[10](#A7.E10 "In Theorem G.1 (Non-identifiability barrier under shifts). ‣ G.2 Formal statement and proof ‣ Appendix G Proof of Theorem (Non-identifiability under environment shifts) ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").
In the target environment (deployment/private), the shortcut correlation
breaks: under $`\theta_{0}`$, $`p_{0}`$ is uniquely optimal; under
$`\theta_{1}`$, $`p_{1}`$ is uniquely optimal, with margin $`\Delta`$,
satisfying equation
[12](#A7.E12 "In Theorem G.1 (Non-identifiability barrier under shifts). ‣ G.2 Formal statement and proof ‣ Appendix G Proof of Theorem (Non-identifiability under environment shifts) ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").
No amount of interaction with $`e_{\mathrm{src}}`$ can identify which
world holds.

#### Example 2: relaxed verification (slack) vs exact verification (constraint shift).

In combinatorial optimization, it is common to evaluate candidate
programs using a *relaxed* verifier (e.g., allowing numerical slack),
then validate with an *exact* verifier. For instance, in circle packing,
one may verify non-overlap with a numerical slack such as $`10^{-6}`$,
and later validate with an exact checker; converting a relaxed-feasible
solution into an exact-feasible one may require tiny but nonzero
modifications, and rankings can change when switching verifiers. This is
explicitly discussed in the context of circle packing verification with
slack vs exact validation. The source environment $`e_{\mathrm{src}}`$
can correspond to the relaxed evaluator, while the target environment
$`e_{\mathrm{tgt}}`$ corresponds to the exact evaluator. Then two
hypotheses $`\theta_{0},\theta_{1}`$ can be constructed so that they are
indistinguishable under the relaxed evaluator for all queried programs,
yet the exact evaluator reverses which program is truly best (with gap
$`\Delta`$), matching Theorem
[G.1](#A7.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem G.1 (Non-identifiability barrier under shifts). ‣ G.2 Formal statement and proof ‣ Appendix G Proof of Theorem (Non-identifiability under environment shifts) ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").

## Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve

This section describes the implementation of ExpEvolve used in our
experiments. Alg.
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
summarizes the search loop, and Alg.
[2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
details the discovery of idea factors. We implement ExpEvolve on the
backbone of SCS ([Gideoni et al., 2026](#bib.bib22)). In each
generation, ExpEvolve generates $`B`$ programs in parallel slots. The
prompt of each slot contains the task instruction, an optional strategy
instruction from an idea-guided action, a summary of the idea memory,
and a few example programs, and the mutator LLM $`G`$ writes a new
program from the prompt. All LLM calls use DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and the
hyperparameters are listed in Table
[3](#A8.T3 "Table 3 ‣ H.4 Idea-Guided Exploration at Plateaus ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").
Each generated program is evaluated once. A program is treated as failed
if the evaluation fails or returns a non-finite objective, and failed
programs are neither repaired nor retried. The LLM calls for generation
are not retried in our experiments either, so a failed call, e.g., due
to rate limits, yields a failed program that still counts toward the
evaluation budget.

Algorithm 2 DiscoverIdeas

### H.1 Idea Memory and Annotation

Idea factors. Each idea factor $`z`$ in the idea memory
$`\mathcal{M}_{t}`$ is stored with a name, a description of its code
pattern, a type, i.e., binary or categorical, and a value set
$`\mathcal{V}`$. The description is also used by the annotator LLM to
recognize the idea factor from the source code. The annotator LLM labels
each program with $`z(p)\in\mathcal{V}\cup\{\mathsf{unknown}\}`$, where
the label is $`\mathsf{unknown}`$ if the idea factor cannot be
recognized. The annotation of a program is a separate LLM call,
independent of the proposal of idea factors, with the source code
truncated to $`4000`$ characters.

Score contrast. For a binary idea factor, the score contrast is the
difference of the mean scores between the successful programs labeled
$`\mathsf{true}`$ and those labeled $`\mathsf{false}`$. For a
categorical idea factor, the score contrast is the difference of the
mean scores between the value with the highest mean score and the value
with the lowest mean score. Programs labeled $`\mathsf{unknown}`$ are
excluded from the score contrast.

Updating the memory. After each generation, UpdateMemory labels the new
programs with all existing idea factors, recomputes the score contrasts,
and merges two idea factors if the Pearson correlation of their labels
on the archive exceeds $`0.85`$ (Alg.
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
line 8). Degenerate evaluations, whose scores collapse to extreme
values, are excluded from the statistics. It also updates the statistics
of the actions (Appendix
[H.3](#A8.SS3 "H.3 Idea-Guided Actions ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")).

Memory summary in the prompt. Every slot, including random exploration,
receives a summary of the idea memory (line 5). The summary lists the
six idea factors with the largest absolute score contrasts, each with
its name, description, direction of effect, numbers of programs with and
without it, and score contrast, and gives the mean score of each value
for categorical idea factors. It also contains the outlier programs that
the current idea factors fail to explain, i.e., one program with a large
positive residual and one with a large negative residual
($`|z|\geq 1.5`$), with their source code truncated to $`1500`$
characters.

### H.2 Idea Discovery

Trigger. Discovery is triggered every $`n_{\mathrm{disc}}`$ generations
after the first generation, when the archive contains at least $`15`$
successful programs and the idea memory contains fewer than $`12`$ idea
factors, excluding the background idea factors (Alg.
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
line 9).

Pairwise ranker. Let $`\sigma_{Y}`$ be the standard deviation of the
scores of the successful programs in the archive. ExpEvolve builds all
pairs of successful programs $`(p,p^{\prime})`$ with
$`|y(p)-y(p^{\prime})|\geq 0.25\,\sigma_{Y}`$, and labels each pair by
$`\mathrm{sign}(y(p)-y(p^{\prime}))`$. The feature of a pair is the
difference of the binary encodings of the idea factors, where a factor
is encoded as $`1`$ if it is labeled $`\mathsf{true}`$ and $`0`$
otherwise, together with the standardized difference of the code lengths
as a covariate. The ranker is a ridge least-squares model without
intercept ($`\lambda=10^{-3}`$), refit in each discovery round.

Selecting unexplained pairs. ExpEvolve selects the pairs that the ranker
orders incorrectly (Alg.
[2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
line 4), and excludes the pairs on which the current idea factors take
identical values. The selected pairs are ranked by
$`\mathrm{acc}_{0}(p,p^{\prime})\cdot w(p,p^{\prime})`$, where
$`w(p,p^{\prime})=1.5`$ if the two programs come from the same
generation and $`1`$ otherwise. The null accuracy
$`\mathrm{acc}_{0}(p,p^{\prime})`$ is the fraction of $`500`$ random
permutations of the scores over programs, under which a ranker refit on
the permuted labels still predicts the true order of the pair. A pair
with a high null accuracy is easy to order from the idea factors, so
that its misranking indicates a missing idea factor. The null accuracy
uses the differences of the idea factors without the code-length
covariate. Up to $`\ell=6`$ pairs are used, with each program appearing
in at most two pairs. If fewer than $`3`$ pairs are available, the
discovery round is skipped. When the idea memory is empty, ExpEvolve
selects the $`\ell`$ pairs with the largest score gaps under the same
constraints (lines 1–2).

Proposing candidates. For each selected pair, the prompt of the proposer
LLM contains the score gap in raw units and in units of $`\sigma_{Y}`$,
the scores, the predicted scores and the residuals of both programs, the
order predicted by the ranker, the idea factors on which the two
programs differ, and the source code of both programs truncated to
$`1500`$ characters each. The proposer LLM is asked to explain the
unexpected order, and proposes $`8`$ candidates in each round, each with
a name, a description, a type, a value set, and a predicted direction
(line 6).

Annotation and admission. Each candidate is annotated on the whole
archive (line 8). ExpEvolve admits a candidate if the two values
compared by its score contrast are each taken by at least $`n_{\min}=5`$
programs, the absolute score contrast is at least
$`\eta=\max(0.25\,\sigma_{Y},\,10^{-3})`$, and the candidate does not
duplicate an idea factor in the memory, an idea factor removed before,
or another selected candidate (line 9). Two idea factors are considered
duplicates if their names are identical, the token Jaccard similarity of
their names is at least $`0.6`$, or the token overlap of their
descriptions is at least $`0.45`$. Since the archive is collected
adaptively by the search, the score contrast is an association within
the archive and does not identify the effect of the idea factor.
Admission therefore makes an idea factor available for testing, and the
search examines it through the actions (Appendix
[H.3](#A8.SS3 "H.3 Idea-Guided Actions ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")).

### H.3 Idea-Guided Actions

Actions. Allocate compiles the idea factors into actions, i.e.,
$`\mathsf{ADD}(z)`$ and $`\mathsf{REMOVE}(z)`$ for a binary idea factor,
and $`\mathsf{SET}(z{=}v)`$ for each value $`v`$ of a categorical idea
factor (Alg.
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
line 3). The action set is rebuilt in every generation, and keeps at
most three actions of the idea factors with the largest absolute score
contrasts, together with a baseline action without instruction. An
action that has stayed in the action set for $`N_{\mathrm{rot}}`$
consecutive generations is rotated out to give way to other actions, and
its records are kept for when it enters the action set again. Before an
admitted idea factor is compiled into actions, its absolute score
contrast must exceed the $`95`$th percentile of a null distribution
obtained from $`200`$ permutations of the scores, and a threshold on the
absolute score contrast is used instead when the permutation test cannot
be run. Background idea factors (Appendix
[H.4](#A8.SS4 "H.4 Idea-Guided Exploration at Plateaus ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"))
are not compiled into actions, until they satisfy the admission
conditions of Appendix
[H.2](#A8.SS2 "H.2 Idea Discovery ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
and are promoted to regular idea factors.

Prompt of an action. An idea-guided slot differs from random exploration
in two parts of the prompt (line 5). First, a strategy instruction asks
the mutator LLM to use or avoid the pattern of $`z`$, or to set $`z`$ to
$`v`$, with the description of $`z`$ and its estimated effect. Second,
the example programs consist of the best program in the archive as an
anchor, followed by the best programs in the target state of the action,
where ties between programs with similar scores are broken in favor of
programs with rare combinations of idea factors, and $`k=3`$ example
programs are used in total. There is no explicit parent program, since
SCS conditions the mutator LLM on a set of example programs.

Random exploration. A random exploration slot uses the prompt of SCS
without strategy instruction, with $`3`$ example programs sampled
uniformly at random from the successful programs, and the summary of the
idea memory.

Diversification in the warm-up. In the warm-up generations, the slots of
the baseline action in the second half of each generation receive a
diversification instruction, which asks the mutator LLM to first list
three to five distinct families of well-established approaches to the
task as code comments, and to note which families the example programs
use.

Allocating slots. In each generation, Allocate assigns
$`\max(2,\mathrm{round}(\rho B))`$ slots to random exploration, and the
remaining slots to idea-guided actions, where $`u_{t,b}`$ denotes the
action of slot $`b`$ and $`u_{t,b}=\bot`$ denotes random exploration
(line 3). An idea-guided slot falls back to random exploration if no
action is available, e.g., before any idea factor is admitted, or if the
actions have reached the limit of slots per generation. The fraction of
random exploration is thus at least $`\rho`$.

Bandit. The bandit selects the actions of idea-guided slots with a soft
UCB rule,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
s(a)=\tilde{r}_{\max}(a)+c\sqrt{\frac{\ln(N_{\mathrm{tot}}+1)}{n_{a}}},\qquad\Pr(a)\propto\exp\big(s(a)\big),
``` |  |

where $`n_{a}`$ is the number of times that $`a`$ has been selected,
$`N_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{a}n_{a}`$, and $`c=1`$. Actions that have not
been selected are tried first. The value $`\tilde{r}_{\max}(a)`$ is the
maximum reward of $`a`$, minus a bootstrap estimate of the expected
maximum of $`n_{a}`$ rewards drawn from all actions, which corrects the
growth of the maximum with the number of samples. The reward of a
program generated under an action follows the normalized reward in Sec.
[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Exploiting Idea Factors for Discovery ‣ 4 ExpEvolve: Discovering and Exploiting Ideas from Experience ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
where the standard deviation is lower bounded as
$`\sigma_{\mathrm{rand}}=\max\big(\mathrm{std}(y_{\mathrm{rand}}),\,0.05\,|\bar{y}_{\mathrm{rand}}|,\,10^{-6}\big)`$
(line 8). If fewer than two random exploration programs are available in
the generation, the adjacent generations are included. A failed program
receives a penalty score below the worst successful program.

### H.4 Idea-Guided Exploration at Plateaus

Entering and leaving a plateau. ExpEvolve records the best-so-far score
at the end of each generation, and the search is in a plateau if the
best-so-far scores of the last $`\kappa+1`$ generations are equal up to
a relative tolerance of $`10^{-4}`$, after the warm-up generations. When
the search enters a plateau, ReviseAtPlateau runs the background probe
and the dependency judge below (Alg.
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
lines 12–13). The plateau ends as soon as the best-so-far score
improves, and all the changes during the plateau are reverted in the
same generation. Each time the search enters a plateau again, the probe
and the judge are run again, since the background of a new plateau can
differ from the previous one.

Background probe. An LLM reads the $`8`$ successful programs with the
highest scores, with the source code truncated to $`1500`$ characters
and the names of the current idea factors, and proposes $`2`$ to $`4`$
binary properties that these programs share. Each property is annotated
on the archive, and is recorded as a background idea factor if at least
$`5`$ of the $`8`$ top programs are annotated and at least $`80\%`$ of
them realize the property. A background idea factor stays in the memory
after the plateau, and is promoted to a regular idea factor once enough
programs without it appear in the archive and its score contrast passes
the admission threshold.

Dependency judge. The background is described by the three idea factors
with the largest absolute score contrasts. For each idea factor in the
memory, and for each value of a categorical idea factor, an LLM judge
decides, with three calls, whether it depends on the background, i.e.,
loses its meaning or reverses its effect once the defining property of
the background no longer holds.

Changes during a plateau. While the search is in a plateau, ExpEvolve
applies the following changes.

- •
  *Reversing and masking actions.* For a binary idea factor judged
  dependent, $`\mathsf{ADD}(z)`$ is replaced by $`\mathsf{REMOVE}(z)`$
  in the action set, with the same description and score contrast, so
  that the bandit can only move away from $`z`$. For a categorical idea
  factor, the actions of the values judged dependent are masked, while
  the other values are kept as escape actions. The dependent idea
  factors are also removed from the summary of the idea memory. After
  the plateau, the original actions are restored, and the records of the
  reversed and masked actions are kept.
- •
  *Stall note.* A note on the current state is prepended to the prompt
  of every slot. The note reports the best score and the number of
  generations without improvement, lists the dependent idea factors with
  their names and shortened descriptions, states that the search has
  stalled on this combination, and asks whether other constructions or
  combinations can reach a higher score.
- •
  *More random exploration.* Each idea-guided slot is reassigned to
  random exploration with probability $`0.9`$. Since the judge runs at
  the end of the first plateau generation, the probability is lowered to
  $`0.3`$ from the next generation.
- •
  *Diversified demonstrations.* Random exploration uses the best program
  of the background as the first example, and fills the other examples
  with programs outside the background, which are selected greedily to
  diversify their idea factors. A program is considered in the
  background if it realizes any dependent idea factor.
- •
  *Exploration of the bandit.* In the first $`2`$ generations of a
  plateau, the bandit selects the actions by the exploration bonus only.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
````
