## Appendix I Experimental Details

### I.1 Tasks

Table
[4](#A9.T4 "Table 4 ‣ I.1 Tasks ‣ Appendix I Experimental Details ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
summarizes the $`11`$ tasks. Nine tasks are the mathematical problems
studied by SCS ([Gideoni et al., 2026](#bib.bib22)), which are taken
from AlphaEvolve ([Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib61)), and we report
their reference values as collected by [Gideoni et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib22). All methods use the same evaluator for each task,
and each evaluation is limited to $`60`$ seconds, except the uncertainty
inequality with $`300`$ seconds.

| Task | Direction | Previous best | AlphaEvolve |
|----|----|----|----|
| First autocorrelation inequality | $`\downarrow`$ | $`1.5098`$ | $`1.5053`$ |
| Second autocorrelation inequality | $`\uparrow`$ | $`0.88922`$ | $`0.8962`$ |
| Uncertainty inequality | $`\downarrow`$ | $`0.3523`$ | $`0.3521`$ |
| Erdős minimum overlap | $`\downarrow`$ | $`0.380927`$ | $`0.380924`$ |
| Sums and differences of sets | $`\uparrow`$ | $`1.14465`$ | $`1.1584`$ |
| Max–min distance ratio ($`16`$ points) | $`\downarrow`$ | $`12.890`$ | $`12.88927`$ |
| Heilbronn for triangles ($`n=11`$) | $`\uparrow`$ | $`0.036`$ | $`0.0365`$ |
| Kissing number ($`11`$ dimensions) | $`\uparrow`$ | $`592`$ | $`593`$ |
| Circle packing ($`26`$ circles) | $`\uparrow`$ | $`2.634`$ | $`2.63586`$ |
| Circle packing via LP ($`26`$ circles) | $`\uparrow`$ | – | – |
| Hadamard matrix ($`n=29`$) | $`\uparrow`$ | $`0.9357`$ | – |

Table 4: Tasks, optimization directions, and reference values. The
previous best values and the values of AlphaEvolve are collected by
[Gideoni et al. (2026)](#bib.bib22). For the uncertainty inequality, all
methods in [Gideoni et al. (2026)](#bib.bib22) reach $`0.3482`$ under
their reformulated parameterization, which we use in our experiments.
For the Hadamard matrix, the previous best is the normalized score of
the best-known construction.

First autocorrelation inequality. Let $`C_{1}`$ be the largest constant
such that $`\max_{t}(f*f)(t)\geq C_{1}\big(\int f\big)^{2}`$ for all
non-negative functions $`f`$ supported on $`[-1/4,1/4]`$, where $`f*f`$
is the autoconvolution. A non-negative step function $`f`$ gives an
upper bound $`C_{1}\leq\max_{t}(f*f)(t)/(\int f)^{2}`$, which the task
minimizes. The number of steps is chosen by the program, and for a step
function with $`n`$ steps and values $`h`$, the score is computed as
$`2n\max(h*h)/(\sum h)^{2}`$, which is invariant to the scale of $`h`$.

Second autocorrelation inequality. Let $`C_{2}`$ be the smallest
constant such that
$`\|f*f\|_{2}^{2}\leq C_{2}\,\|f*f\|_{1}\,\|f*f\|_{\infty}`$ for all
non-negative functions $`f`$. A non-negative step function $`f`$ gives a
lower bound $`C_{2}\geq\|f*f\|_{2}^{2}/(\|f*f\|_{1}\|f*f\|_{\infty})`$,
which the task maximizes. The evaluator rejects step functions with more
than $`10^{4}`$ steps.

Uncertainty inequality. For a function $`g`$, let
$`A(g)=\inf\{r>0:g(x)\geq 0\text{ for all }|x|\geq r\}`$. For even
functions $`f`$ with $`f(0)\leq 0`$ and $`\hat{f}(0)\leq 0`$, the task
minimizes $`A(f)A(\hat{f})`$, which upper bounds the largest constant
$`C`$ such that $`A(f)A(\hat{f})\geq C`$. Following the reformulation of
[Gideoni et al. (2026)](#bib.bib22), $`f`$ is a Hermite–Gaussian
expansion over the monic (probabilist’s) Hermite polynomials
$`H_{0},H_{4},\dots,H_{28}`$ with $`7`$ free coefficients, which
represents a larger class of functions than the original formulation
over $`H_{0},H_{4},H_{8},H_{12}`$ with $`3`$ free coefficients. The sign
conditions are checked on a grid of $`2\times 10^{5}`$ points in
$`[10^{-6},30]`$, which is refined to $`2\times 10^{6}`$ points with
extended precision when the score is below $`0.6`$, and each evaluation
is limited to $`300`$ seconds. Since the reformulation enlarges the
search space, the resulting values are not comparable with the values of
the original formulation in Table
[4](#A9.T4 "Table 4 ‣ I.1 Tasks ‣ Appendix I Experimental Details ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").
In the implementation, the score is $`r^{2}/(2\pi)`$, where $`r`$ is the
largest root at which $`f`$ changes sign.

Erdős minimum overlap problem. For a partition of $`\{1,\dots,2n\}`$
into two sets $`A`$ and $`B`$ of equal size, let
$`M(n)=\min_{A,B}\max_{k}|\{(a,b)\in A\times B:a-b=k\}|`$. The task
constructs a step function $`h`$ with values in $`[0,1]`$, whose number
of steps is chosen by the program, and minimizes the upper bound on
$`\lim_{n\to\infty}M(n)/n`$ given by twice the maximum correlation
between $`h`$ and $`1-h`$ divided by the number of steps.

Sums and differences of sets. Following the framework of Gyarmati,
Hennecart, and Ruzsa, the task constructs a set
$`U\subset\mathbb{N}_{\geq 0}`$ with $`0\in U`$ that maximizes
$`\theta(U)=1+\log(|U-U|/|U+U|)/\log(2\max(U)+1)`$, which lower bounds
the largest exponent $`\theta`$ such that
$`|A-B|\geq c(K)|A+B|^{\theta}`$ for arbitrarily large sets $`A,B`$ with
$`|A+B|\leq K|A|`$.

Max–min distance ratio. The task places $`16`$ points in the plane to
minimize the squared ratio between the maximum and the minimum pairwise
distances. For example, the squared ratios $`12.889`$ and $`13.0`$ in
Table
[1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
correspond to the ratios $`3.5902`$ and $`3.6056`$.

Heilbronn problem for triangles. The task places $`11`$ points in the
equilateral triangle with vertices $`(0,0)`$, $`(1,0)`$, and
$`(1/2,\sqrt{3}/2)`$ to maximize the smallest area of the triangles
formed by any three of the points, normalized by the area $`\sqrt{3}/4`$
of the equilateral triangle.

Kissing number in $`11`$ dimensions. A set of points
$`C\subset\mathbb{R}^{11}`$ with $`0\notin C`$ and
$`\min_{x\neq y}\|x-y\|\geq\max_{x}\|x\|`$ over $`x,y\in C`$ yields a
kissing configuration of $`|C|`$ unit spheres. The task constructs such
a set, and the score is the number of points $`|C|`$. The distances and
norms are only used to check the validity of the configuration, and a
configuration with more points than the known upper bound $`868`$ is
rejected.

Circle packing. The task places $`26`$ non-overlapping circles in the
unit square to maximize the sum of their radii. The evaluator checks the
non-overlap and the containment of all circles, including that every
radius is at most $`0.5`$ and every center lies in the unit square, and
checks that the sum of radii reported by the program agrees with the
radii up to a relative and absolute tolerance of $`10^{-3}`$.

Circle packing via linear programming. A variant of circle packing where
the program proposes only the $`26`$ centers $`C_{i}\in[0,1]^{2}`$, and
the radii are recovered by a linear program that maximizes
$`\sum_{i}r_{i}`$ subject to $`r_{i}+r_{j}\leq\|C_{i}-C_{j}\|`$ and
$`r_{i}\leq\min(C_{i}^{x},C_{i}^{y},1-C_{i}^{x},1-C_{i}^{y})`$. The
variant isolates the layout of the circles from the assignment of the
radii. The starting code in the prompt solves the linear program with
the HiGHS solver of SciPy.

Hadamard matrix. The task constructs a matrix
$`H\in\{\pm 1\}^{29\times 29}`$ that maximizes
$`|\det(H)|/(2^{28}\cdot 7^{12}\cdot 342)`$. Following the convention of
[Wang et al. (2026)](#bib.bib96), the best-known construction with
$`|\det(H)|=2^{28}\cdot 7^{12}\cdot 320`$ scores
$`320/342\approx 0.9357`$.

### I.2 Baselines

SCS. We use the implementation of SCS ([Gideoni et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22)), which generates each program from a prompt
containing the task instruction and $`3`$ example programs sampled
uniformly at random without replacement from the archive. SCS does not
maintain an idea memory, and its prompt does not contain the summary of
the idea memory used by ExpEvolve.

SCS+meta. SCS+meta adds the meta-summary of ShinkaEvolve to the prompt
of SCS, i.e., a textual summary of the insights of recent programs with
at most $`5`$ recommendations, which is rewritten by DeepSeek-V4-Flash
at temperature $`0`$ after every generation, without the idea memory,
the idea-guided actions, and the exploration at plateaus of ExpEvolve.
It is run on First autocorrelation, Heilbronn, and Kissing with $`10`$
generations of $`20`$ programs, and on Uncertainty inequality with
$`20`$ generations of $`10`$ programs.

ShinkaEvolve. We run ShinkaEvolve ([Lange et al., 2026](#bib.bib37))
with $`5`$ islands and migration every $`10`$ generations, weighted
parent sampling, an archive of $`40`$ programs, a meta-summary every
$`10`$ generations with $`5`$ recommendations, and both diff-based and
full rewrites. ShinkaEvolve generates one program per generation, and
does not distinguish the two configurations of ExpEvolve and SCS.

### I.3 Budget and Resources

All methods evaluate each generated program once, and a failed program
consumes the budget. The LLM calls of ExpEvolve for proposing,
annotating, probing, and judging idea factors do not evaluate programs
and do not consume the budget. Each run of ShinkaEvolve starts from
$`5`$ copies of the initial program, one for each island, and then
generates $`199`$ programs, so its final performance is reported at
$`199`$ generated programs. The evaluations of ExpEvolve and SCS are not
limited in CPUs, while the runs of ShinkaEvolve on First
autocorrelation, Second autocorrelation, Kissing, and Max–min distance
ratio evaluate each program with at most $`8`$ CPUs. The LLM is accessed
either through the official API of DeepSeek or through OpenRouter,
depending on the time of the run.

### K.1 More Details of Experiments on Machine Learning Engineering

We further study whether the effectiveness of ExpEvolve transfers to
machine learning engineering (MLE). We integrate its idea discovery and
search control into OpenRSI ([Yang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib102)) and
evaluate the resulting agent on MLS-Bench ([Lyu et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib54)). This setting examines the use of idea factors
within a harness that supports evolution on ML algorithms towards a
specific task objective.

Tasks and data. MLS-Bench evaluates agents on improving components of ML
algorithms under fixed task interfaces and evaluation protocols. Here we
consider 6 tasks: *Online bandit*, *Anomaly detection*, *Clustering*,
*Multi-objective optimization*, *Subgroup calibration shift*, and
*Evolution strategy*. Search leverages the scores and execution feedback
exposed by each task.

Backbone and budget. We use the evolutionary harness from OpenRSI, which
organizes search through Draft, Improve, Debug, and Crossover operators.
For each task, we retain a fixed history containing 20 completed search
slots from an earlier OpenRSI run. The OpenRSI baseline and OpenRSI
equipped with ExpEvolve continue from this same history for 50
additional evaluator calls, with 3 seeds. Both methods use 5 search
slots per generation. All program generation uses Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. The
same checkpoint performs factor discovery and annotation in ExpEvolve.

Integrating idea factors with OpenRSI. ExpEvolve initializes its idea
memory from the shared history and updates it with newly evaluated
programs. Consistent with Sec.
[4](#S4 "4 ExpEvolve: Discovering and Exploiting Ideas from Experience ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
Discovery examines program pairs whose score differences are
insufficiently explained by the current factors. The LLM reads their
source and proposes reusable mechanisms. Factors $`z`$ enter the action
catalog when both states have sufficient support and exhibit a score
contrast in the archive. Each generation reserves two slots for Open
exploration and schedules three for Guided search. Specifically, A
guided slot first selects an action, such as $`\mathsf{ADD}(z)`$ or
$`\mathsf{REMOVE}(z)`$, and then the harness selects a high-scoring
parent compatible with that change. We use improvement over the best
selected parent as action feedback, adapting the reward reference to
OpenRSI’s parent–child structure. When the cumulative best score remains
unchanged within relative tolerance $`10^{-4}`$ across three generation
boundaries, ExpEvolve switches to idea-guided exploration at plateaus,
aligning with Sec.
[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Exploiting Idea Factors for Discovery ‣ 4 ExpEvolve: Discovering and Exploiting Ideas from Experience ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").

Evaluation and results. We evaluate search performance using the
best-so-far (BSF) score. For each task and method, we average the final
BSF score over three seeds, starting from the same 20-slot history and
continuing for 50 additional evaluations. Fig.
[9(a)](#S5.F9.sf1 "In Figure 9 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
compares OpenRSI with OpenRSI+ExpEvolve across the six tasks. The
reported configurations improve the mean final BSF score on all six
tasks, with the largest gains on Online bandit and Anomaly detection.

## Ethics Statement

This work studies evolutionary coding agents on open-ended mathematical
discovery tasks and on machine learning tasks from MLS-Bench. It does
not involve human subjects or personally identifiable information, and
all tasks come from public benchmarks or prior work.

## Reproducibility Statement

The full procedure of ExpEvolve is given in Alg.
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
and Alg.
[2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
and its implementation details and hyperparameters are given in Appendix
[H](#A8 "Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")
and Table
[3](#A8.T3 "Table 3 ‣ H.4 Idea-Guided Exploration at Plateaus ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery").
The tasks, evaluators, and reference values are described in Appendix
[I.1](#A9.SS1 "I.1 Tasks ‣ Appendix I Experimental Details ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
the configurations of the baselines in Appendix
[I.2](#A9.SS2 "I.2 Baselines ‣ Appendix I Experimental Details ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),
the budget and resources in Appendix
[I.3](#A9.SS3 "I.3 Budget and Resources ‣ Appendix I Experimental Details ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery"),

[E](#A5 "Appendix E Proof of Theorem (Structured experience reuse) ‣ ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery")

## AI Use Statement

We used LLM assistance to revise the manuscript’s organization and
wording, identify and check related references, and examine the
interpretation of reported experiments. The proposed framework itself
uses LLMs to generate programs, propose idea factors, and assess program
properties.
